adventure.title: A Wedding for the River
adventure.synopsis: Three evenings before Tomas Vale marries Neris Reed-in-Rain, Mera Quill opens the two sealed readings of their compact. The ceremonial lines match. The marriages in the margins do not. Tomas and Neris settled rooms, work, water, and care in ordinary speech, then let their elders choose public words large enough to honor both houses. Both households chose a formula shaped by the flood that killed Perrin Vale. The Vales hear a river bride entering the mill and keeping its dead. The river kin hear a miller entering the current and becoming answerable to warnings that once stopped at his gate. Their gifts carry the same double edge: a white veil honors the dead and buries a river bride; a closed iron ring records a brother's labor and promises captivity; a handstone offers steadiness and a fixed course. Meanwhile, twelve protected trout leak across the market because a cousin embroidered a joke until somebody believed him. The adventurers serve as free witnesses. They may question, compare, pause, and propose. They may not choose the marriage. Their task is to discover what each word, gift, duty, and public act will do, return every choice to Tomas and Neris, and sign no more than they can honestly witness. No villain opposes the wedding. Love, haste, old grief, and good intentions are enough.
adventure.premise: You carry the seal of the House of Open Measure and owe no debt on either bank. At the opening of the three-day witness period, Tomas Vale and Neris Reed-in-Rain's two sealed household readings are opened together. Their central words agree; their meanings do not. The wedding is set for the evening when low sun strikes the wet mill wheel. By then, two households have built different marriages out of the same compact, gifts, names, feast, and ceremony. Your office permits questions, comparison, private repetition, pauses, proposed forms, and a scoped signature. It does not permit you to decide for the couple. Move among mill, willow house, market, shrine, reed yard, music bridge, and flood meadow. Find what the old words conceal, what the new promises cost on an ordinary day, and what Tomas and Neris still choose when every beautiful thing has been explained.
adventure.explanation:
The Concord of Banks governs agreements where mortal settlements meet the old households of rivers, woods, roads, and hills. Its House of Open Measure does not reconcile those households or make their customs interchangeable. It records the places where they touch: who speaks, who acts, who may refuse, what changes hands, and where a duty ends. The finished record must survive an unfriendly reader without becoming stronger than the people who signed it.

For a cross-bank marriage, each household files a sealed reading copy before the three-day witness period. The ceremonial lines are known in advance. The marginal gloss—what those lines confer, require, and preserve—remains sealed until both copies are opened together. Neither side can revise its reading after seeing the other. The rule prevents opportunistic editing; it also lets an honest contradiction appear late. Mera Quill received both filings and will draft the final folio. She cannot independently certify the record she kept and wrote, so the House appoints free witnesses with no kinship, lease, inheritance, debt, or old-flood quarrel on either bank.

Tomas Vale runs the Cresswater mill with his widowed sister Mara. He thinks in gates, shifts, rooms, repairs, and notices. He expects the eastern rooms to become the couple's ordinary home. Neris Reed-in-Rain keeps spawning records and flood warnings along the lower channels. She expects to share those rooms while retaining the willow house as a home whose duties may call her without permission. Tomas calls this one household in two dwellings. Neris calls it two continuing households joined by marriage. Their keys and schedules nearly agree. Their nouns do not, and those nouns govern recognition, care, authority, and future claims.

The compact's old formula is bound to the flood that killed Perrin Vale. The Vales hear it bringing Neris into the mill's living and dead without conveying the mill away from them. The river household hears it binding Tomas to warnings that once died at the wheelhouse threshold. Each side chose the same words because each believed those words repaired the flood's unfinished duty. The contradiction is not a mistranslation. It is one grief carrying two remedies.

The families prepare with materials they trust. Agnes Vale brings a white flax veil that welcomed brides and later covered her drowned husband. Serein-at-Alderfall asks Tomas to enter river kinship because a warning that stops at the mill gate is useless. Orren Underbridge has spent six nights forging a closed iron ring. Mara offers a handstone while keeping deed, wages, water lease, and succession in separate books. Rain-at-Noon carries the cracked bell from the flood and wants a warning handoff that works when the grieving elders are absent. None is secretly hostile. Each may be generous while asking the couple to inhabit a meaning they never chose.

The calendar creates pressure, not authority. The wedding may be postponed. Food can be served, platforms stored, gifts returned, and another date chosen. The joining light will not return for a year, and disappointment will harden into public stories, but postponement kills nobody.

At the Market of Seven Baskets, hospitality becomes names, appetites, chairs, beds, labor, sources, gifts, abstentions, and debts. Pella Nine-Spoons refuses to cook for “river folk” as one imaginary stomach. Protected trout must return to the channel. Deep-Reed needs a dry chair with moving water at her feet; Noll Ferry needs a dry bed; Lilt-before-Storm needs to hear current but not sleep in it. Shared food may arrive in separate courses. Attendance, eating, dancing, and silence never become assent by implication.

At the Shrine of the Open Door, Keeper Ansel reduces the ceremony to six acts: consent, household standing, names, exchange, promises, and departure. Dessa Reedwright gives those acts footing, sight lines, handrails, water return, named labor, and a rain route. Iven Crossbow and Moss-in-Evening decide who leads, who answers, where four and six meet, and where music must stop. A veil, ring, boat, refrain, or procession has no office until its giver declares one and its receiver accepts it.

The flood-meadow rehearsal puts every elegant plan under weight. Chairs arrive. Children move markers. Water cuts another channel. Food waits. Agnes cannot hear in the wheelhouse. Deep-Reed cannot turn where the drawing says she should. The old flood is rebuilt from high-water cuts, a cracked bell, delivery marks, a lost path, and duties nobody had agreed to receive. The result may be a three-signal warning chain, separate true statements, a later hearing, or no joint act. Forgiveness is not a wedding supply.

The finale displays the state the table actually made. Footing shows whose body was considered. Names show what remains stable and what may change. Gifts show which intentions were accepted, altered, withheld, or returned. Silence marks the places where no crowd may answer. The departure shows whether the threshold boat receives Tomas into kinship, removes him from the mill, or has no place at all. The folio separates consent, household standing, property, office, adoption, care, exchange, promises, open matters, adaptations, abstentions, and the scope of each signature.

A successful ending may remain rough. Tomas and Neris may keep two household descriptions beside one working schedule. Agnes and Serein may sign different lines. River adoption may be bounded or deferred. A gift may stay home. A grievance may move to another hearing. The couple may proceed without House certification, postpone, or end the process. The witnesses succeed when no difference hides inside a shared word and every remaining edge belongs to someone who knowingly chose it.

Keep four structures distinct at the table. The calendar determines when rehearsal and wedding occur. The clue graph locates evidence and examples. The authority graph shows who may commit a person, office, property, labor, or household. The ceremony state records what Tomas and Neris have accepted. A skipped encounter narrows evidence; it does not lock a door. A late fact reopens only the affected act. An absent principal may be consulted, never impersonated. Each witness signs what they observed or later verified, and nothing else.

references.title: Tomas Vale
references.summary: A practical miller who wants to marry Neris, keep his Vale belonging, and accept only river duties precise enough to survive an ordinary Tuesday.
references.content:
## Work and manner

Tomas Vale is thirty, broad through the shoulders, patient with machinery, and slow to notice when other people have mistaken his silence for consent. He runs the Cresswater mill with his widowed sister Mara. He promises gates opened, rooms repaired, and shifts covered; ask for a declaration and he asks which ordinary day must survive it.

## What he wants

Tomas wants to marry Neris and make the mill's eastern rooms their ordinary shared dwelling. He expects river work to call either partner elsewhere, but initially describes the willow house as another beloved home rather than a second continuing household. He will become river kin when the warning, evacuation, closure, rescue, and hearing duties are exact. He will not trade one belonging for another.

## Authority and limits

Tomas may consent to the marriage, accept personal river duties, and agree to changes in his own work and residence. He cannot answer for Neris, confer Vale property or succession by himself, bind Mara or the mill workers to unnamed labor, or turn marriage into authority over river work. He remains Tomas Vale unless he later earns and accepts a river byname.

references.title: Neris Reed-in-Rain
references.summary: A lower-channel current-keeper who wants to marry Tomas without surrendering her river work, willow-house standing, changing names, or right to object.
references.content:
## Work and manner

Neris Reed-in-Rain keeps spawning records, negotiates closures, and carries warnings along the lower channels. She is river-born, not immortal, and not the Cresswater speaking through one mouth. She hears consequences quickly, though beautiful language can make her wait too long before objecting.

## What she wants

Neris wants to marry Tomas and share the mill's eastern rooms while retaining the House Beneath the Willows as a home whose duties may call her without permission. She wants both continuing households recognized rather than one home treated as real and the other as an absence. She will not become the sole translator, symbolic bridge, or living water lease between them.

## Identity, authority, and limits

Neris presently answers to Reed-in-Rain. Her stable witness identity also preserves her parentage, earlier child-name, and dwellings; later bynames append rather than erase. She may consent to marriage, residence, personal promises, and her own use of names and gifts. She cannot confer river-household adoption, speak for every river guest, transfer the mill, or commit another person's care, labor, or grievance.

references.title: Mera Quill
references.summary: The House of Open Measure recorder who preserves the paired filings and drafts the folio but cannot replace an independent witness or answer for a principal.
references.content:
## Office

Mera Quill is the resident recorder of the House of Open Measure. She received the two sealed household readings, opens them together, preserves the paired record, advises on form, and drafts the final folio. Because she kept the filings and will write the instrument, she cannot also serve as the independent field witness who certifies it.

## Working practice

Mera separates observed, proposed, accepted, contested, refused, and unasked matters. She records people and offices separately, protects private consent checks, preserves different signature scopes, and can schedule a later hearing for a clause that does not belong inside the wedding.

## Authority and limits

Mera may explain House procedure, maintain registers, test whether wording is operable, and refuse to enter knowingly incompatible or unchosen meanings as one certifiable term. She cannot choose the marriage, fill a pause, accept for an absent principal, turn family assent into personal consent, or make her own observation stand in for the free witnesses'.

references.title: Agnes Vale
references.summary: Tomas’s grandmother, keeper of the white veil, and a principal bearer of Vale memory from the flood that killed Perrin.
references.content:
## Place in the household

Agnes Vale is Tomas's grandmother. She wants Neris welcomed into the Vale sequence without Tomas, Perrin, or the household dead being politely erased. The white flax veil is both her own wedding heirloom and the cloth later laid over her drowned husband.

## The veil and the flood

Agnes offers continuity, not conquest, but fear can make her speak as though the gift already has an accepted office. She remembers Perrin remaining at the wheel after the river warning came too late to become a received command. Her memory is true and incomplete; it need not become Serein's memory before the warning system can be repaired.

## Authority and limits

Agnes may offer, transform, keep private, or withhold the veil. She may give testimony, attend, abstain, or state the Vale remembrance she accepts. She has no right to Neris's face, name, residence, burial, work, or consent, and she cannot make Perrin's grief a condition of the marriage.

references.title: Serein-at-Alderfall
references.summary: Neris’s mother and a senior current-keeper whose office can confer river adoption only through exact, reciprocal, bounded duties.
references.content:
## Household and office

Serein-at-Alderfall is Neris's mother and a senior current-keeper. She keeps current records and speaks for adoption within her office. Ask for a blessing and she speaks like water over stone; ask who must answer a black reed knot at midnight and every word acquires an edge.

## What she wants

Serein wants Tomas directly answerable to warnings, closures, evacuation, rescue, and hearing so river obligations no longer stop at the mill gate. She accepts that he may live mainly at the mill, remain Vale kin, retain his property and trade, and refuse danger beyond the duties he actually undertakes. Adoption that supplies only ceremonial praise is not adoption to her.

## Authority and limits

Serein may accept, condition, or refuse river adoption and reciprocal commitments belonging to her office. She cannot answer for Neris's marriage, transfer Vale property, erase Tomas's mortal kinship, impose unrestricted labor, or make the wedding settle the old flood. Her account of Perrin's death is true without being the only true account.

references.title: Mara Vale
references.summary: Tomas’s widowed sister and co-operator of the Cresswater mill, generous toward Neris but exact about which welcome, labor, property, care, and succession promises she has authority to make.
references.content:
## Work and manner

Mara Vale is thirty-four, widowed, and responsible for the mill’s accounts, purchases, wages, repairs, tenant quarrels, and the work Tomas volunteers himself to do twice. She judges flour by touch, reads lateness in the knots on grain sacks, and distrusts any beautiful sentence that hides an unnamed shift or liability.

## What she offers

Mara welcomes Neris as a true resident of the eastern rooms, with keys, domestic authority, household purchasing, a worker-council seat, and a water-compliance role. She recognizes the willow house as another continuing dwelling. She can assign mill hands within safe limits, help implement the paired warning protocol, and revise the handstone’s public use with Neris.

## Authority and limits

Mara may bind her own labor and the mill operations entrusted to her. She may not transfer Tomas’s property, the Concord water lease, worker wages, debt, Elsin’s future, or the whole mill through a wedding clause. Care duties must name the people accepting them. Her caution is not hostility to the river household; it is refusal to let welcome become an unpriced claim on workers, tenants, or a child.

references.title: Orren Underbridge
references.summary: Neris’s elder brother, a repairer of gates and hinges whose six nights of worked iron must be acknowledged and corrected without turning care into confinement.
references.content:
## Craft and manner

Orren Underbridge repairs fish gates, bridge shoes, and water hinges. He speaks in conclusions and becomes clumsy when a sentence approaches tenderness. He trusts labor that leaves its joints visible and worries that the mortal bank will praise river kin at the wedding, then curse the first closure that costs flour.

## The worked-iron gift

Orren forged a closed ring from a flood-gate fitting as an attempt to learn a mortal wedding form for his sister. Among his own kin, the closed circle can mean containment, debt without outlet, and a promise unable to breathe. Neris will not wear it. Orren can open it into a spiral, divide it into clasps, leave a rush-bound gap, place it in a threshold, or withhold it. He will not melt away the six nights of mistaken care merely to make the error disappear.

## Authority and limits

Orren controls his craft, his gift, and the labor he personally accepts. He can lead platform lifting, bridge pegging, rescue, and craft teaching. He cannot answer for Neris, confer river adoption, assign the wider household, or make his gift necessary to the marriage. Correction must preserve both the receiver’s refusal and the maker’s truthful labor.

references.title: Rain-at-Noon
references.summary: Serein’s younger sister, a dry-witted warning carrier and grievance steward who keeps the cracked mill bell as proof that a sign sent is not yet a sign received.
references.content:
## Work and manner

Rain-at-Noon carries warnings, verifies river source marks, and speaks with jokes dry enough that mortals sometimes wait for a punch line that has already passed. During the old flood she carried river signs toward the mill and came away with a cracked yard bell. She keeps it because warning is a completed handoff only when somebody receives, understands, acknowledges, and acts.

## Grievances and the old flood

Rain can steward a bounded grievance: speaker, respondent, unfinished duty, next act, date, and later hearing, without a judgment of character. She will keep Perrin Vale’s death out of a wedding feast interval, accept stewards, and send it to a separate hearing. She will not say no warning was sent, assign the death wholly to the Vales, or perform reconciliation for ceremonial neatness.

## Authority and limits

Rain may carry and translate warnings, verify intake and return points, teach warning lore, operate the paired protocol, and accept or decline a public grievance entry. She cannot confer adoption, speak for Neris or Serein, promise regular care, or turn the cracked bell into a verdict. Her preferred settlement is practical: paired river and mill measures, named keepers on both banks, acknowledgment, escalation, and a rule for absence.

references.title: The House of Open Measure
references.summary: The Concord of Banks witness office that records where unlike households touch, preserving consent, authority, refusal, limits, and endings without reconciling the households or deciding for them.
references.content:
## Two doors, one record

The House of Open Measure is the Concord of Banks office for agreements where mortal settlements meet old households of river, wood, road, and hill. Its local seat has two doors and no privileged entrance. The House does not make customs interchangeable. It records the exact places where they touch and writes for the unfriendly absent reader who might otherwise enlarge a promise.

## What survives the absent reader

A sound folio separates stable identity, current answered names, parentage, dwellings, household standing, property, labor, care, warnings, gifts, abstentions, open clauses, and the authority behind each assent. Free witnesses observe or verify the acts; a resident recorder preserves filings and drafts the resulting forms. Refusal, postponement, asymmetry, and a named later hearing are recordable outcomes rather than procedural failures.

## The seal and its edge

The House may receive paired readings, commission or recognize independent witnesses, preserve revisions, and certify only what qualified witnesses observed. Its seal opens doors and earns answers. It confers no judgment over love, household, mill, river, marriage, or grief. A recorder who accepted the filings and drafts the folio cannot also become the independent witness who certifies it.

references.title: Vale Mill and Hearth
references.summary: A working Cresswater mill, multigenerational Vale home, and leased water operation where every wedding promise must survive workers, tenants, debt, flood signals, and an ordinary week.
references.content:
## Wheel, hearth, and lease

Vale Mill and Hearth is a workplace before it is a family emblem. The wheelhouse shakes flour from the rafters; the bake room begins before dawn; six workers and four tenant households order their weeks around the sluice, stones, deliveries, and account books. The Vales own buildings and machinery, while the right to divert Cresswater belongs to a renewable Concord lease with separate signatures and remedies.

## The eastern rooms

The eastern rooms are Tomas and Neris’s intended ordinary dwelling, with a common room, yard door, runnel steps, and space for current ledgers and river tools. Full domestic welcome does not transfer mill ownership, wages, debt, succession, or the water lease. The willow house remains another recognized dwelling, and no count of nights determines loyalty or abandonment.

## Where promises become shifts

At the mill, promises become keys, shifts, warning thresholds, closure authority, care instructions, and somebody awake beside the wheel. Property, operation, household authority, and water compliance remain distinct. The place remembers the old flood in high-water cuts and a jammed lower gate without settling blame. A workable compact must protect people before machinery and continue when Tomas or Neris is absent.

references.title: The House Beneath the Willows
references.summary: A river household beneath a broad willow reach: Neris’s continuing home, Serein’s adoption office, and the place where kinship becomes named warning, rescue, care, grievance, and hearing duties.
references.content:
## Beneath the willows

The House Beneath the Willows occupies a broad root-bound reach open to current and air. Stepping stones and low platforms join sleeping shelves, reed pens, mussel baskets, silt pigments, and ledgers weighted beneath glass. It is a household, not a court. Neris belongs here as daughter, sister, current-keeper, and principal rather than as an envoy between banks.

## Duties that travel

Serein speaks for adoption within her office; Orren repairs gates and hinges; Rain carries warnings and stewards bounded grievances. Adoption can add exact warning, closure, evacuation, rescue, and mixed-hearing duties without requiring permanent residence or erasing mortal kinship. The household owes reciprocal signals, current readings, aid, recovery, review, and honest thresholds.

## What the current cannot claim

The willow house remains Neris’s continuing dwelling after marriage and may receive Tomas under its rules. Care may occur here by choice or necessity without becoming custody. The household cannot claim mill property, Mara, workers, future children, unrestricted labor, or Neris’s personal consent. Its gifts, adoption, testimony, and recognition may each be offered, revised, deferred, or withheld by the person who holds that authority.

encounters.title: The House of Open Measure
encounters.summary: Two identical compacts lie beneath two river stones. Their three sentences place Tomas and Neris in different homes, offices, names, and lines of care.
encounters.opening_view: Mera Quill waits until the alder leaf has passed beneath the table before she speaks. “These are the same words.” Two wedding compacts lie under smooth river stones, identical down to the last stroke; the notes in their margins would make two different marriages. Four ledgers remain closed beside them. The folio meant to hold the witnesses’ account is blank. Mera keeps her hands behind her back, as though even touching the page might answer a question that is not hers.
encounters.content:
## Situation
The **House of Open Measure** stands where alder shade gives way to the mill channel: a square, whitewashed room with two doors and no privileged entrance. Dry benches face a public copying table. Scales hang on one wall. A shallow runnel comes through the river door, passes beneath the table, and leaves by the road.

The adventurers are the **free witnesses**. The regular circuit is trapped at an upstream boundary hearing, and the three-day witness period has begun without them. Mera may receive filings, preserve the paired record, advise on form, and draft the folio. Because she accepted the readings and will write the folio, she may not also serve as the independent field witness who certifies it. The adventurers might belong to the traveling circuit, carry its seal after earlier service, or simply be the nearest credible outsiders. Their qualification is mostly absence: no kin here, no water lease, no inheritance, no household debt, no share in the old flood quarrel.

Mera Quill gives them four duties:

1. ask whether **Tomas Vale** and **Neris Reed-in-Rain** choose this marriage now;
2. find the customs, gifts, words, and public acts that do different work on opposite banks;
3. write the meaning the principals accept, with its bearer, limit, refusal, and ending; and
4. sign only those acts they observe or later verify.

The seal opens doors and earns answers. It confers no judgment over love, household, mill, river, or marriage. The witnesses may call a pause. They may not fill it.

## The contradiction on the table

**Mera Quill**, the resident recorder, has placed two copies of the compact side by side. Six weeks ago, each household lodged a sealed reading copy with her. The shared ceremonial lines were known; the margins explaining how each household expected those lines to operate were not. Concord practice opens the copies together at the beginning of the witness period so neither side can revise its gloss after seeing the other's. The protection worked. The disagreement is visible and attributable—but late.

The copied text is identical:

> Tomas enters the house of Neris. Neris keeps the wheel. Each bears the other's name before water and flame.

The mortal Vale household reads the first sentence as ceremonial courtesy before Neris enters Tomas's hearth. The river household reads it as Tomas's adoption into Neris's current. The Vales read “keeps the wheel” as Neris becoming mistress of the mill. The river kin read it as a promise that the mill wheel will remain answerable to the river and never become the bride's private property. “Bears the other's name” is equally unstable: mortal records expect a fixed household name, while river bynames change with season, deed, grief, and residence.

Nobody forged the document. Nobody hid a clause. Tomas and Neris signed a notice of intended marriage and agreed on many ordinary arrangements; they did not approve either household's marginal claims. They asked their elders to choose the ceremonial formula because neither wanted marriage to look like a rejection of the household that had formed them, especially after Perrin Vale's death. Each assumed their practical agreement would govern any grand words. That was a shared evasion, not a trap.

The same flood made the old formula attractive to both sides. The Vales hear Neris entering their hearth, keeping the wheel, and preserving Perrin's place among the household dead. The river kin hear Tomas entering a current of reciprocal duty and making the wheel answer warnings that once died at its threshold. One sentence appears to mend the same wound in opposite directions.

Mera will not send forward for certification a compact whose words can place two people in different households at the same instant. The wedding is three evenings away, when the lowering sun passes through the old wheel and lays a bright path from the mill yard to the willow bank. The date is not an apocalyptic deadline. The feast can be eaten, guests can go home, and the couple can marry next year. But postponement would publicly harden every present doubt: that Tomas is surrendering the mill, that Neris is being captured on dry land, or that their affection could not survive plain speech.

## The couple are not one position

Tomas and Neris want the wedding. They do not want precisely the same marriage, and neither has yet found language that keeps the other from paying for the difference.

Tomas answers pressure by fixing the nearest thing. At Mera's table he calls the eastern rooms “our home” and the willow house “her other home,” then stops when Neris repeats the possessives. He will accept exact warning, closure, rescue, and hearing duties. He will not exchange Vale belonging for river belonging or let a generous promise quietly assign Mara and the mill workers.

Neris corrects him without withdrawing from the rooms they have prepared. She expects to sleep there most ordinary nights and beneath the willows when current work requires it. What she refuses is the idea that one dwelling becomes real while the other survives by permission. She will not spend the marriage translating every river warning, relative, and claim through herself.

Their keys and schedules already fit better than their descriptions. Neither wants marriage or adoption to move the mill, the water lease, or inherited obligations. The live disagreement is whether they are one household in two dwellings or two continuing households joined by marriage. That difference reaches warning duties, care, names, future claims, and who may speak when one principal is absent. The witnesses must make those consequences explicit without choosing the description for them.

## Mera Quill
Ink has worked permanently into the side of Mera's left hand, but she keeps that hand off the blank folio while the witnesses speak. The grander a compromise grows, the quieter she becomes. Then she turns the page sideways and asks:

- Who acts?
- Who may refuse?
- What event calls the duty?
- What ends it?
- How will the person carrying flour tomorrow say this without changing it?

She will compare precedents and draft more than one honest form. She will not announce a best answer. If the witnesses settle everything with the families and return for a ceremonial yes, Mera closes the folio, reties the red cord, and says, “You have recorded everybody except the people marrying. Begin again.”

## The private consent procedure

The House uses a four-pass procedure whenever household interests may make public agreement easier than honest disagreement. Run it at least once during the first day and again, briefly, before the ceremony.

### 1. Separate desire

Question Tomas and Neris in different rooms, beyond relatives and gifts. Ask whether each wishes to marry **now**, not merely whether each loves the other or once promised to marry. Either may request postponement without giving the other household a public reason. The witnesses record only “free,” “conditional,” “not yet,” or “refused” unless the speaker asks for more detail to be shared.

### 2. Separate terms

For each unsettled subject—residence, adoption, mill work, water duty, names, care, children, death, and postponement—ask for four answers:

- what the speaker positively wants;
- what the speaker can accept;
- what the speaker will not accept; and
- what the speaker does not yet understand well enough to promise.

Silence, embarrassment, deference, and “whatever Neris wants” or “whatever keeps the Vales easy” are not consent. They are prompts for a more exact question.

### 3. Reciprocal paraphrase

Bring the couple together. Each must describe one material obligation the other is accepting and one limit the other is retaining. Perfect legal language is unnecessary. A paraphrase fails only when the listener says, “That is not what I meant,” or when it leaves out the person who must bear the cost.

### 4. Repeated choice

After the witnesses draft possible language, question the couple again. A private answer becomes part of the compact only when its speaker repeats or adopts it in the other's presence. Changing an answer is evidence that the procedure worked, not evidence of unreliability.

Compelled speech, read thoughts, and truth-punishing magic answer the wrong question. The House needs a choice the speaker understands and may revise, not metaphysical proof of sincerity.

## Their first separate answers

These answers establish live tensions. They are starting positions, not predetermined solutions.

| Subject | Tomas | Neris |
|---|---|---|
| Marriage now | Yes, if Neris is not being asked to become the mill's living lease | Yes, if river adoption is a real obligation rather than ceremonial decoration |
| Ordinary residence | The eastern rooms are their home; duty may take either elsewhere | The eastern rooms and willow house are both homes; neither requires leave from the other |
| Mill standing | Neris may share management by agreement but receives no ownership or inherited debt by marriage | She wants authority over household matters and water compliance, not title to machinery |
| River adoption | He accepts defined warning, evacuation, spawning, rescue, and hearing duties | He must be answerable beyond the wheel gate, but not generally commandable by her kin |
| Names | He remains Tomas Vale and will accept a river byname only if later earned | She keeps an acknowledged chain of river names and will use “of Vale Mill” as an address, not a replacement surname |
| Future children | No household should claim them by default; he wants them secure in the mortal registry | Both households must owe care; household standing should be chosen later, not fixed at birth |
| Incapacity or death | The surviving partner keeps the eastern rooms and may call on both households for care | Neither family may remove an incapacitated spouse without that person's prior direction or the other's agreement |
| Postponement | Painful but preferable to a promise Neris cannot safely paraphrase | Acceptable if one of them needs it; she will not permit the families to call delay abandonment |

Do not copy this table into a contract. Test every answer at the mill, beneath the willows, and against an ordinary week.

## Terms that can become clauses

The following modules are available once the party has learned enough to propose them. They are not a canonical settlement; Tomas and Neris may combine, revise, or reject them.

### Household and residence

- The eastern rooms are the couple's shared dwelling at the mill.
- The willow house remains Neris's household standing and a second dwelling available to both partners.
- Neither partner requires permission to answer an existing duty at another dwelling.
- An absence does not become abandonment unless the absent partner refuses an agreed request for contact or hearing.

The couple must still decide whether the record calls this **one household in two dwellings** or **two households joined by marriage**. The practical duties can be identical while the recognition differs.

### Mill and water

- Mill buildings, machinery, debts, wages, and mortal succession remain under the Vale deed and account books.
- Water diversion, spawning closure, drought restriction, and flood-warning duties remain under the Concord lease.
- Neris may act as the mill household's named water correspondent without becoming owner or debtor.
- Tomas may not invoke marriage to speak for the river household beyond duties it explicitly assigns him.

### Adoption duties

Tomas may accept a bounded set of duties:

1. answer one of three recognized warning signals;
2. stop the wheel and open the lower sluice when the agreed flood threshold is met;
3. ring the mortal bell and help clear workers, tenants, and animals from the yard;
4. honor posted spawning closures and prevent mill employees from evading them;
5. carry or relay downstream warnings when able;
6. accept rescue and appear at a mixed hearing before using force in a water dispute.

Adoption does not transfer property, cancel Vale kinship, impose unrestricted labor, require Tomas to enter dangerous water beyond his ability, or let one household conceal a warning from the other.

### Names

A stable record may read:

> Neris, child of Serein-at-Alderfall, entered in the House index under her unchanging witness mark, presently answering to Reed-in-Rain and dwelling also at Vale Mill.

Later bynames append to the chain rather than overwrite it. “Neris of Vale Mill” may describe residence. “Neris Vale” is used only if she freely chooses it, which she presently does not. Tomas remains Tomas Vale. No river byname is invented for the wedding; one may be recorded if later earned and accepted.

### Care and future children

- Each partner may call on either household for urgent care.
- Neither household gains default custody of an ill, injured, or grieving spouse.
- A future child is entered in the mortal birth register and the river care ledger without either entry deciding permanent household standing.
- Named adults from both households owe food, rescue, shelter, and notice.
- No immersion, apprenticeship, change of name, removal from a dwelling, or assignment of inheritance occurs merely because one household claims custom.
- Household standing may be revisited when the child can understand the choice; property succession remains governed by the relevant deed rather than by river adoption.

Name the adult who accepts each care duty. “Both families will help” is not a clause.

## Immediate problems

Before the witnesses can finish reading, three preparations arrive at once.

- **Agnes Vale**, Tomas's grandmother, brings her wedding veil and announces that Neris will wear it.
- **Orren Underbridge**, Neris's elder brother, brings a polished iron ring and asks whether the dry folk truly intend to close metal around his sister.
- A market runner reports that the feast committee has ordered twelve river trout from the protected spawning reach because “river guests must want river fish.”

Each problem is sincere, visible, and reversible. No lore check supplies the correct culture. Learn what the giver meant, what the receiver hears, and whether another use can preserve the gift without preserving the injury.

## Starting movement

Mera recommends that the party divide their attention between the two households before the market closes. Tomas can guide them through the mill. Neris can bring them safely beneath the willows. The compact remains at the House under paired stones, and either family may add proposed language in a separate margin; nobody may alter the common text without both betrothed present.

The House remains available for comparison, private consent checks, and revised drafts. A return should clarify the record, never solve it by authority.

## Running the commission out of order

Mera draws four narrow columns beside the compact: **observed**, **proposed**, **accepted**, and **contested**. She keeps two smaller marks for **refused** and **unasked**. These are not grades. They prevent a useful idea from becoming a promise merely because several people discussed it.

After the opening contradiction is clear, all six preparation sites are available. The market, shrine, yard, bridge, mill, and willow house are ordinary places with known roads and expected hours. The clue graph records where the witnesses can learn useful conclusions and corroborate them; it does not create locked doors. The rehearsal and wedding are scheduled in advance. A party can arrive at either with unfinished work.

If the witnesses divide, each group may observe, ask questions, reserve reversible resources, draft wording, and carry offers. A group cannot accept for an absent principal or household officer. On reunion, each group answers four questions:

1. What did you directly observe?
2. What did you propose?
3. Who accepted the exact proposal, and within what authority?
4. What remains refused, conditional, contested, or unasked?

Mera records where Tomas, Neris, and traveling principals actually are. A named person does not appear in two simultaneous scenes because a dramatic answer would be convenient. Messages take the time and route the table has established. A witness who did not observe a private answer may later verify it only through explicit repetition, not through another witness's confidence.

The House remains open for private questions and revised drafts, but returning after every encounter is unnecessary. Bring the compact back when a term requires reciprocal paraphrase, a speaker requests privacy, authority is disputed, or the witnesses need to compare incompatible records. Otherwise, the common ledger can travel with paired witness marks and be reconciled at the next actual meeting.

## One-sided cooperation

The House separates six matters that families often compress into one word: personal marriage, Vale household standing, river household standing, river adoption, mill authority, and House certification. Each may have a different answer.

If the Vale household cooperates and the river household does not, Tomas and Neris may still marry as individuals. Neris retains her existing river standing, but Tomas is not adopted and the river household owes no unaccepted reciprocal duties. If the river household cooperates and the Vales do not, Tomas may accept exact river duties, but Neris gains no Vale property, office, debt, succession, or household recognition by implication. If both households withhold recognition, the couple may still exchange personal promises and depart together; the House may witness that ceremony while declining cross-bank household certification.

Internal division is ordinary. Agnes may lend the veil while Mara refuses an operational clause. Orren may give an open ring while Serein defers adoption. Record people and offices separately. Nobody may turn "the family" into an imaginary unanimous speaker.

A household officer may withhold only what belongs to that office: property, labor, recognition, reciprocal duty, participation, testimony, or signature. Such a refusal changes the ceremony state. It does not answer whether Tomas and Neris marry. The witnesses similarly control only the scope of their own certification.

## Failure forward

A failed consent scene does not reveal that the relationship was secretly false. It exposes a term that is not ready. Mark it as conditional, return it to the relevant encounter, or leave it for a later hearing. If one partner requests postponement, the House protects that choice without requiring an accusation. If the couple proceeds without resolving a clause, Mera can record the exact boundary. If one partner cannot freely answer “yes” at the final repetition, the witnesses cannot certify the wedding even if affection and every preparation remain intact.

## The hospitality appendix

Mera’s first guest sheet has two broad columns: “Vale” and “river.” Both are crossed out. The replacement register names each person and separates ceremony attendance, feast attendance, lodging, food, access, abstention, gift, and grievance roles.

Mera explains that household affiliation is useful for invitation authority but almost useless for accommodation. The House will record who confirmed each entry and whether a guest’s presence extends to a particular rite. Attendance at the wedding does not imply participation in every course, grievance, gift, or dance.

The register keeps the couple from becoming universal translators. Pella, Mera, hosts, and stewards carry named responsibilities. Neris does not spend her wedding explaining every river guest; Tomas does not answer for every Vale relative because he knows their names.

encounters.title: Vale Mill and Hearth
encounters.summary: At the mill, flour, wages, a water lease, a white veil, a handstone, and a child's chalked shift board force welcome into exact terms.
encounters.opening_view: Before anyone can say marriage, the mill says work. The floor shudders; flour drifts through the window bars; water shoulders the wheel around once more. Agnes Vale spreads a white veil across sacks marked by three generations of the same hand. Mara does not sit. She sets down a deed, a wage book, a water lease, care instructions, and a ring of new keys, one by one. “Tell me,” she says, “which of these does a wedding carry?”
encounters.content:
## Situation
The Vale mill is a workplace before it is a family emblem. The wheelhouse shakes flour from the rafters. The bake room begins before dawn. Six hired workers and four tenant households order their weeks around the sluice, the stones, and Mara Vale's account books. The Vales own the buildings and machinery; the right to divert Cresswater lives in a renewable Concord lease with different signatures and remedies.

The household is preparing the wedding through things it knows how to prepare. Benches have been borrowed. Wheat and red thread mark every lintel. The eastern rooms have been scrubbed and aired. Agnes has unfolded the white veil. Mara has set deed, wage book, lease, and care instructions on separate corners of the same table. Each act is generous. Each also answers a question Tomas and Neris have not finished asking.

At the mill, every promise must survive a working week. Who takes freeze watch? Who tells customers when spawning closure stops the wheel? Where do Neris's current ledgers live? Who may spend household money, halt machinery, assign a worker, or promise a room? What happens when river duty and a profitable grain run call at the same hour? Welcome becomes keys, shifts, signatures, and somebody awake beside the wheel.

## Agnes Vale and the veil
Agnes lays the white flax veil over the grain sacks and keeps smoothing one old crease. She wore it at her wedding and later placed it over Perrin's body after the flood. To the Vales, joy and mourning may travel in the same heirloom. To Neris's kin, cloth over the face can mean breath withheld and a person removed from current.

Agnes wants Neris to receive the best-kept object of the Vale women and to speak Perrin's name before the river guests. Fear makes that offer sound larger than she intends. The cloth can become canopy, compact wrapping, threshold lining, an act begun with Tomas and opened by Neris, or a private memorial kept at home.

Ask Agnes what she is giving. Ask Neris what use she can receive. If no use carries both answers, the veil stays folded without turning refusal into insult.

## Mara Vale and the mill
Mara keeps moving between the table and the wheelhouse. Each time somebody says *welcome*, she puts a different book beneath the word: wages, debt, the water lease, Elsin's care instructions, next week's shifts. The marriage changes the mill even if no deed moves, because Tomas has been covering extra wheel work since Mara's husband died.

She needs notice when river duty takes Tomas downstream, authority named before a spawning closure interrupts a profitable run, and a fallback when both principals are absent. She offers Neris keys, equal domestic standing in the eastern rooms, household purchasing, a worker-council seat, and water-compliance work. She also recognizes the willow house as a continuing dwelling. None of those offers transfers wages, debt, succession, or the whole mill.

Asked whom she trusts, Mara says, “Neris when Neris speaks for herself. I am still learning which of her mother's promises arrive wearing Neris's name.”

## Elsin Vale is not an inheritance token

**Elsin Vale** is twelve, carries chalk behind one ear, and has memorized the sluice ratios. Adults point to her whenever they want succession to sound settled. She likes mill work. She may inherit it, manage it, or leave it. The compact must protect the place she has without turning a child's present answer into a life sentence.

Elsin can show the witnesses four separate ledgers:

- the deed book for buildings and machinery;
- the wage and debt accounts;
- the Concord water lease;
- and Mara's private care instructions naming who should house Elsin if Mara dies while she is still young.

The last ledger matters. It names Tomas first, Agnes second, and two unrelated neighbors after them. It does not award Elsin to “the Vale household” as an abstract body. Mara chose particular people and may revise the list. This provides a model for future care: duties belong to named people who accept them, not automatically to whichever household claims the stronger custom.

Elsin can concede the ceremonial phrase “Neris keeps the wheel” if everyone states that it means water accountability rather than succession. She is delighted by the idea of Neris teaching her to read current marks. She will not stand silently in the ceremony as proof that succession is solved, and she will correct anyone who says the mill is already hers.

A witness who asks Elsin what she fears receives a practical answer: “That they will promise each other every hour they have, and Mara will put my name in the empty shifts.”

## The wheel, lease, and four kinds of authority

The mill's human succession is simpler than rumor suggests. Tomas and Mara jointly operate it. Mara owns a larger share of the buildings under their parents' deed; Tomas owns the wheel machinery and part of the grain store. Elsin is a likely future successor but no present owner. The river lease belongs to the operating mill and must be renewed by its named managers with the consent of the mixed water hearing.

Workers are nevertheless worried. **Hobb Fen**, the senior mill hand, has heard that river spouses claim whatever turns in water. **Lysa Cart**, who delivers flour, has heard the opposite: that Neris will be required to stand aside while Tomas's kin use her name to renew the lease forever. Both rumors convert a marriage into a property seizure because nobody has stated the boundaries aloud.

Keep four kinds of authority separate:

1. **Property:** ownership of buildings, machinery, stored grain, and debt remains where the deed and accounts place it.
2. **Operation:** Tomas and Mara continue assigning shifts, wages, orders, and repairs unless they separately admit another manager.
3. **Household:** Tomas and Neris share authority over their dwelling, food, guests, care, and purchases without that authority extending automatically to the whole mill.
4. **Water compliance:** Neris may issue or relay closures and warnings in her current-keeper capacity; Tomas accepts specified duties under adoption and lease.

Neris can therefore be a full member of the domestic household, an acknowledged water correspondent, and a respected participant in worker councils without becoming owner, debtor, universal manager, or living embodiment of the lease.

## Tomas under ordinary pressure

Question Tomas while something needs repair. Split a grain sack, stick a gate, or send a worker for next week's shifts. He solves the immediate problem first. Then he says, “We can manage,” by which he means that he will quietly absorb the collision.

Press him gently on concrete collisions:

- If a spawning closure begins during a profitable milling run, he will stop the wheel once the signal and threshold are verified.
- If the flood signal sounds, he will open the lower sluice, ring the bell, and help clear workers and tenants before protecting machinery.
- If Neris must remain beneath the willows for a week, he will not treat her absence as withdrawal from the marriage.
- If both river duty and mill duty require him, he wants Mara or the named shift leader to hold the mill while he fulfills the warning duty.
- He will not promise to enter deep floodwater, leave vulnerable workers without warning, or obey an unnamed messenger who cannot identify the signal.

Tomas need not choose Neris against his family. He must learn that “I will take care of it” often means Mara, Neris, or a future Tomas will pay. Make him name who acts when he cannot.

## Residence, rooms, and care

The eastern range has two bedrooms, a small common room, a door into the mill yard, and stone steps descending to the runnel. Tomas has repaired the steps for Neris. He has not noticed that every storage chest is labeled “Vale East,” every guest assumes the willow house is being left behind, and Agnes has begun planning which river cousins may visit rather than recognizing them as Neris's household.

Separate welcome from absorption:

- Neris receives keys and equal domestic authority in the eastern rooms.
- Her current ledgers and river tools have dedicated space rather than being treated as temporary belongings.
- The willow house remains a recognized dwelling for Neris and is available to Tomas by its household rules.
- No count of nights determines loyalty, inheritance, or abandonment.
- If either partner is incapacitated, prior directions and the other partner's voice govern where care occurs; neither family may simply remove its relative.
- If one partner dies, the survivor retains the eastern rooms for an agreed period or for life, depending on the couple's choice, without acquiring the dead partner's unrelated property by default.

Mara is open to a lifetime dwelling right for Neris if Tomas dies, provided it is tied to the eastern rooms and domestic garden rather than the entire mill. Serein will later ask for an equivalent assurance that Tomas may receive care beneath the willows without surrendering himself to river custody.

## The stone gift

Mara has commissioned a small ceremonial millstone as the Vale household's principal gift. To mortals, a stone with a clean central eye means steadiness, labor, and a household fed by repeated work. To river folk, a pierced stone presented to a bride can mean that her course is fixed and her voice made to turn another household's machinery.

Mara will be wounded if told that the gift is simply offensive. She chose it because she respects Neris's practical work. She is open to altering its use: the stone might become the base of the public water bowl, a table at the shared threshold, or one half of a paired gift whose other half moves freely.

Mara will not present the stone as a title to Neris's labor or as proof that Neris “keeps the wheel” in every sense. If the witnesses distinguish the meanings well, Mara may ask Neris to choose its public use herself.

Mara's workshop inventory already provides the bones of an honest declaration. It names her as owner and giver, the retired millstone as source, the mason as maker, the shared water bowl as the proposed use, and return to Mara if Neris refuses it. The line for permitted alteration is still blank. Filling that line with Neris is more useful than asking either household what a pierced stone means in general.

## Productive scenes

- Tomas shows the witnesses the eastern rooms and admits that he has promised each family that “nothing important will change.”
- Mara produces the four ledgers and asks whether Neris will sign as household member, water representative, both, or neither.
- Agnes asks one adventurer to tell her, plainly, whether the river family considers Tomas beneath them.
- Elsin demonstrates how the mill can stop without closing the river channel, a practical image for separating household continuity from control of the water.
- Hobb asks whether he takes a flood order from Neris as Tomas's wife or as a current-keeper; the correct answer may be the latter, and the distinction matters.
- A private conversation with Tomas reveals that he is willing to postpone but dreads telling Agnes because he believes she will hear postponement as a verdict on Perrin.

## Household outcomes

Leave the mill with positions, not a capitulation.

- Agnes may offer the veil in transformed use, keep it while accepting another remembrance, or attend without publicly recognizing the new household.
- Mara may grant Neris domestic authority and a water role while keeping ownership and succession separate.
- Elsin may join the water-reading lesson, refuse ceremonial use as “heir,” or offer the care ledger as a model.
- Tomas may accept exact flood duties, revise his work schedule, and publicly acknowledge two homes even if he still prefers to call the eastern rooms the household's center.

## If the mill is skipped or reached late

The wedding does not wait behind the mill door. If the witnesses never visit, Tomas can still state his personal consent, names, residence intention, and promises. What they cannot presume is Vale household recognition, use of Agnes's veil, Mara's operational commitment, a change in mill authority, or any transfer of property, debt, or succession.

At joining light, ask Tomas which rooms, goods, and duties he personally controls. Anything beyond that remains open unless the actual authority holder answers. The eastern rooms may be recorded as a dwelling Tomas offers within his authority; they do not become proof that Mara accepted Neris into mill management or that the Vale deed changed. The ceremony may omit the veil, use it only if Agnes has separately released it, and state no common Vale household standing.

If the encounter is reached after plans have hardened, bring only the affected choices back for correction. Mara may narrow an operational clause without reopening names or feast arrangements. Agnes may withdraw the veil without undoing Neris's consent. Elsin's observation may correct how adults describe care without making her responsible for deciding inheritance. Late mill evidence changes the smallest relevant scope.

## Failure forward

A quarrel here gives the wedding sharper edges. Agnes may withhold the veil; workers may demand lease language; Mara may keep the stone; Elsin may refuse ceremonial use; Tomas may contradict his family in public. Carry the cost forward. Do not smooth it away.

If the party accepts vague reassurance, the mill remains operational but the unresolved labor appears later: an unstaffed shift, a disputed closure order, or a witness unable to paraphrase who acts during a flood. Make the cost visible before the ceremony so the couple can revise rather than be ambushed afterward.

## Agnes’s seat and the guest register

When Pella’s guest sheet reaches the mill, somebody has written “best elder place” beside Agnes’s name. Agnes strikes it out. What she needs is a stable chair, low background noise, and a clear view of the speaker’s face. At the wheelhouse she hears almost nothing; at a ceremonial head table beside musicians she would miss the vows while appearing honored.

Agnes’s correction is a useful hospitality clue. Her need belongs to Agnes, not to “mortal elders.” Aunt Sal walks farther and hears better but wants a handrail on wet ground. Elsin needs no special seat and resents being placed with children too young to follow the ceremony. The Vale household can confirm names and needs, but each affected person should answer where possible.

encounters.title: The House Beneath the Willows
encounters.summary: Under the willow roots, Serein names the price of adoption, Orren opens the ring he forged, Neris defends two homes, and Rain asks for a warning that reaches a human hand.
encounters.opening_view: Here, a name is not spoken at once. Serein waits while the ripples from your arrival travel beneath sleeping shelves and ledgers sealed under glass. Only when the water lies still does she offer welcome. The house has no walls, only willow roots, green channels, and low platforms joined by stepping stones. On the central platform sit a closed iron ring, a cracked handbell, and a little boat tied between two posts. The bell is old. The knot is new.
encounters.content:
## Situation
Willow roots make rooms open to current and air. Mortals enter by stepping stones and low platforms; shoes stay dry only through attention. Mussel-shell baskets hang beside reed pens, silt pigments stand in stoppered jars, and ledgers rest under glass with stones on their corners.

This is Neris's household, not a river court assembled to receive outsiders. Serein orders duty stones near the adoption boat. Orren keeps the closed iron ring wrapped in rush. Rain-at-Noon has set the cracked mill bell beside the grievance stones. Deep-Reed, Brin Quickwater, and several cousins interrupt one another with the untidy freedom of kin. Here Neris is daughter, sister, current-keeper, and principal—not an envoy hired to translate everyone else.

For every prepared object or duty, ask what changes after the ceremony and what the household owes in return. Who carries a warning when Neris is absent? Who may command dangerous work? What counts as home? Which name survives in a mortal index when her byname changes? The water makes every answer sound fluid. Find the hand that must carry it.

## Serein-at-Alderfall and exact adoption
Alder seeds cling to Serein's hair while she places six duty stones in a row. She does not want a ceremonial son or a promise that the mill will vaguely “honor the river.” She wants recognized warnings to reach somebody already bound to answer them.

Serein states the boundary before anyone asks: Tomas remains Vale kin, keeps property and trade, lives chiefly at the mill, and may refuse danger beyond the duties he undertakes. The adoption gives no command over Mara, Elsin, workers, grain, machinery, or future children.

Asked whether she wants Tomas to belong to her, Serein says, “No. I want his answer to travel farther than his gate, and ours to reach him before the yard is water.”

## Adoption without possession

River adoption does not normally require permanent residence. A person adopted by a current may still keep another hearth, trade, office, lineage, and property succession. The obligation is practical: answer flood calls, protect spawning closures, carry warnings downstream, accept rescue, and submit disputes concerning the water to a mixed hearing before using force.

Orren explains this badly. He says, “The river will know where Tomas belongs,” which sounds to mortals like a custody claim. What he means is that Tomas should no longer be treated as an outside lessee whose obligations stop at the wheel gate.

The household can offer Tomas a bounded adoption with six duties:

1. recognize three agreed warning signals: alder-seed braid for rising water, three struck shells for a sudden gate failure, and a black reed knot for spawning closure;
2. stop the wheel and open the lower sluice when the specified flood mark is reached;
3. ring the mill bell and help evacuate workers, tenants, and animals;
4. prevent employees and guests under his authority from violating a posted closure;
5. carry or relay a warning when he can do so without abandoning people already in danger; and
6. accept rescue and attend a mixed hearing before force, seizure, or deliberate obstruction in a water dispute.

The river household owes reciprocal duties:

1. deliver warnings through an agreed signal and, when possible, a named messenger;
2. give Tomas and Mara access to current readings relevant to mill operation;
3. aid evacuation rather than limiting rescue to river kin;
4. provide food, shelter, and recovery after service or injury;
5. hear a claim that a warning was late, unclear, or impossible to obey; and
6. never conceal a closure or threshold in order to test Tomas's loyalty.

Adoption does not transfer Tomas's property, cancel his mortal kinship, impose unrestricted labor, require him to enter deep current, grant Serein control of his work schedule, or assign future children to the river household.

Tomas must decide whether he accepts these duties. Neris must decide whether she accepts a marriage in which Tomas may remain most nights at the mill and sometimes fail at a river obligation without that failure becoming proof that he never belonged.

## Neris in her own household
At the mill, people mistake Neris for the river's single speaking mouth. Beneath the willows she is a daughter, sister, niece, current-keeper, and sometimes the youngest person in the room. Question her where no relative can hear.

Neris wants Tomas adopted. She does not want to become his interpreter, guarantor, or excuse. River officers should address him directly; mill workers should heed her warning because she holds the office, not because she married the miller. She also rejects the cousins' assumption that pregnancy, injury, grief, or quarrel would automatically return her to willow custody.

Most ordinary meals, possessions, and guests will gather in the eastern rooms. Neris still refuses to call the willow house a former home or to ask permission when its duties call. She says **two households joined by marriage**. Tomas says **one household in two dwellings**. Their keys and schedules may agree. Do not call the difference harmless merely because no deed turns on it.

Alone, Neris says:

> I do not need Tomas to sleep in the water. I need him not to call me absent when I am where my work and my people are. I do not need the mill to become river property. I need its promises to continue when I am not beside the wheel translating them.

## Orren Underbridge and the ring
Orren unwraps six nights of work and presents a closed iron ring made from a flood-gate fitting. He meant to learn a mortal wedding form for his sister. He did not know that the same shape can mean containment, debt without outlet, and a promise unable to breathe among his own kin. Neris will not wear it, and has delayed saying so because every hammer mark is her brother's care.

Orren can open the ring into a spiral, divide it into clasps, leave a rush-bound gap, set it into a threshold, or keep metal off Neris's body. He will not melt the work merely so the mistake vanishes. A witness who works beside him hears the fear beneath that refusal: “They will praise the river at the wedding and curse the first closure that costs them flour.”

## Names that move

Neris's childhood name was **Neris Minnow-Follows**. She became **Neris Reed-in-Rain** after keeping the lower reed beds open during a three-day storm. Her byname may change again. Mortal law, however, needs a stable entry for inheritance, testimony, taxation, and later cross-reference.

Serein objects to “Neris Vale” because it makes her daughter's river name sound discarded. Mera Quill objects to a record that changes without trace. Both concerns can be satisfied by distinguishing a stable witness identity from current bynames and places of residence.

Neris accepts a registry entry that identifies her through parentage, witness mark, and a chain of acknowledged names. She accepts “of Vale Mill” as an address when she is acting from the eastern rooms. She does not presently choose Vale as a replacement surname. This refusal is not a rejection of Tomas or Agnes.

Tomas also faces a name question. River adoption customarily grants a byname after a deed, not at the ceremony. Several cousins have proposed comic names in advance: Tomas Flour-in-Hair, Tomas Wheel-Stops-Late, and Tomas Almost-Dry. Neris wants no ceremonial nickname imposed merely to make the symmetry look tidy. Serein agrees. If Tomas later earns and accepts a river byname, Mera can append it to his record without replacing Vale.

## Rain-at-Noon and the speaking of grievances
Rain-at-Noon places Agnes's broken market basket beside the cracked yard bell. One proves a debt can be bounded: object, creditor, repair, date. The other proves a warning is unfinished until somebody receives, understands, acknowledges, and acts.

She will keep the old flood out of the public feast interval, accept stewards, and assign it to another hearing. She will not erase the river warnings, make Perrin's death wholly a Vale fault, or perform reconciliation because a musician has found a pleasing cadence.

Her useful wedding gift is a conversion board: river marks beside bell times, one named keeper on each bank, and a rule for what happens when the first keeper does not answer.

## The old flood

Serein and Agnes have not spoken directly in nineteen years. During the spring flood, river messengers warned the mill to open its lower gate. Agnes's husband **Perrin Vale** stayed to save the main wheel and died when a timber struck him. Agnes remembers a warning delivered after the yard was already underwater. Serein remembers three earlier signs that the mill dismissed because each used river measures rather than bell times.

Neither woman invented her memory. The failure lay partly in translation and partly in Perrin's choice. The first alder braid was hung where no night worker knew to look. A second warning used current depth without converting it to the mill's carved yard marks. Rain finally carried a bell, by which time evacuation remained possible but the wheel was already endangered. Perrin sent others away and stayed.

Let the flood deepen the wedding without turning it into a solved mystery. A shared acknowledgment may help; forced forgiveness will not. The practical settlement is a warning protocol that works without Neris translating. Agnes may never forgive Serein. Serein may never accept blame for Perrin's last choice. Both may still recognize a better handoff.

## Care, children, and claims of return

River households do not divide care cleanly from belonging. A person rescued, fed through illness, or sheltered after grief acquires obligations of acknowledgment and later aid. Mortal relatives may hear this as a claim over the person. River kin may hear mortal guardianship documents as permission to exclude everyone not named.

Serein's first instinct is that Neris should return beneath the willows for any serious illness because the household understands river-born bodies. Mara's first instinct is that Neris's spouse should decide where the couple receives care. Neris rejects both defaults. She wants prior directions, Tomas's voice when she cannot speak, and room for river expertise without removal from the marriage household.

A care agreement may say:

- either partner may seek care in either dwelling;
- the conscious person chooses where care occurs;
- if a person cannot choose, prior written directions and the spouse's judgment govern unless immediate survival requires otherwise;
- both households receive notice and may offer named help;
- helping with care creates gratitude and reciprocal aid, not custody or property rights;
- the surviving spouse retains agreed dwelling rights without automatically inheriting unrelated household property.

Future children present the same issue in advance. Tomas and Neris agree that no child should be assigned exclusively to one bank at birth. They are open to a mortal registry entry and a river care entry, provided neither is treated as a final household choice. Both households may owe shelter, food, warning, rescue, and teaching. Immersion, apprenticeship, inheritance, naming, and permanent residence require later, separate decisions.

Serein can accept this if specific adults sign the care duties and if a future child is not prevented from learning river marks. Mara can accept it if care status does not rewrite the mill deed or displace Elsin. Orren volunteers rescue and craft teaching. Rain volunteers warning lore but refuses regular infant care, saying that even rivers know their banks.

The couple need not decide whether they will have children. They do need to prevent the compact's household language from assigning hypothetical children without their consent.

## Productive scenes

- Neris asks to be questioned alone about residence, names, children, and the possibility of postponement.
- Tomas is asked whether he accepts the six flood duties and whether he can repeat the river household's reciprocal duties.
- Serein lays six duty stones beside six reciprocal shells and removes any pair whose terms remain vague.
- Orren proudly presents the ring and watches the room become careful.
- Rain-at-Noon demonstrates grievance custom by naming the basket debt she owes Agnes.
- A cousin tries to grant Tomas a comic byname; Neris stops the ritual before the witnesses need to intervene.
- Serein asks whether a future grandchild will be “allowed to know the current.” The useful answer is not reassurance but a named teaching duty that leaves household standing open.

## Household outcomes

Leave with a durable position, even if it is not harmony.

- Serein offers a bounded adoption with public limits and reciprocal obligations.
- Tomas accepts some or all duties, asks for revision, or declines adoption while still marrying Neris.
- Neris secures two-home recognition, or accepts one-household language with explicit equal access and no abandonment by absence.
- Orren transforms the ring while preserving its material history.
- Rain assigns the old flood to a later hearing and contributes a new warning protocol.
- The household signs named care duties without claiming future children or an incapacitated spouse.

Do not require every river relative to accept one symbolic description. Serein may say one household in two dwellings while Neris says two households joined. The record can preserve both if the duties are exact.

## If the willow house is skipped or reached late

Neris does not need her household to answer whether she marries. She may retain her current name, existing river standing, willow-house home, and personal promises. Without direct river-household authority, however, the witnesses cannot record Tomas as adopted, bind reciprocal warning or rescue duties, assume Orren gives the ring, or claim Serein recognizes the marriage on behalf of the household.

The safe fallback is marriage without adoption. State Neris's retained standing, Tomas's unaltered Vale kinship, and any personal water duties he can accept without pretending to hold a river office. Put adoption and reciprocal household duties into a named later hearing or leave them explicitly uncompleted.

If Serein, Orren, Rain-at-Noon, or another river principal arrives late, each may alter only their own sphere. Serein may accept or refuse adoption; Orren may offer, transform, or withhold the ring; Rain may steward a grievance or decline a public entry. Their answers do not travel backward to invalidate unrelated functions already completed. Pause and repeat consent only when the late term changes what Tomas or Neris understood themselves to be choosing.

## Failure forward

The river household may refuse the ring, reject a fixed surname, limit or refuse the public adoption, insist on a separate grievance rite, or decline to sign a care clause. These are not breakdowns. They make the final design more explicit and may cost symmetry, time, or one family's sense of recognition.

If Tomas cannot accept the adoption duties, Neris decides whether marriage without adoption still meets her terms. If Neris cannot secure recognized access to both homes, Tomas decides whether he can change his understanding or whether the couple postpones. If care remains vague, the witnesses can exclude it from the marriage compact and schedule a later hearing rather than allowing either household's default to control silently.

## Deep-Reed’s basin chair

Serein’s elder cousin **Deep-Reed** arrives while the guest list is being discussed. Her knees no longer tolerate crouching on roots, and deep water numbs one leg. She wants a backed chair on dry matting with her bare feet resting in a shallow basin through which fresh water moves. She laughs at the market note assigning all river elders submerged seats.

Beside her, **Noll Ferry** asks for a dry shrine bed because damp air worsens an old lung injury, while **Lilt-before-Storm** says any cot will do if she can hear running water. Their needs contradict one another without either being less river-born. Serein insists that the market record their names rather than turn one accommodation into a custom for everyone.
