encounters.title: The Market of Seven Baskets
encounters.summary: Pella Nine-Spoons empties seven baskets onto the market tables until every claim about hospitality becomes a name, source, seat, bed, task, gift, abstention, or debt.
encounters.opening_view: The first trout hits the floor before Pella Nine-Spoons finishes saying good morning. By the time it is back in the leaking tank, water has reached three separate purses and a guest list so corrected that several names have acquired tributaries. Seven labeled baskets hang overhead. Pella rescues her pencil with her teeth, kicks a stack of borrowed plates out of danger, and points to the open spiral of iron on the table. “Fish first,” she says. “Then relatives.”
encounters.content:
## Situation
The market stands where the mill road, ferry path, and lower channel meet. Every wedding plan eventually arrives here as weight, heat, distance, bedding, crockery, or unpaid work. Pella Nine-Spoons has hung seven scrubbed baskets from the rafters and written one question on each: **who, from where, carried by whom, seated where, sleeping where, given for what, and still owed what**.

The immediate problem has fins. Twelve protected spawning trout circle a wicker tank beside the fountain because Brin Quickwater told Pella, in the grave tone of an archivist, that river guests eat only fish. The tank leaks. The fish must return to moving water before any other feast discussion deserves attention. Returning them introduces the market's governing rule: food has a source, taking creates an obligation, and hospitality begins before the plate.

Pella has room, labor, and fuel for a generous feast, but not for an imaginary one. The guest list counts households where it needs names. The seating plan awards rank where it needs hearing and turning room. Lodging assumes every river guest wants wet quarters. Gifts have been entered as honors before receivers know what they are asked to mean. A grievance custom has been allotted “as long as needed,” which is how soup becomes cold and resentment becomes entertainment.

Do not make the feast uniform. Make every accommodation, refusal, and abstention belong to a named person.

## Pella Nine-Spoons
Pella is broad-shouldered, flour-dusted, and rarely holds fewer than two writing spoons. She earned her byname during a winter flood, when she fed nine stranded ferrymen from one pot after making each confess what he could not eat.

She wants hot food served hot, every source named, every worker credited, every invited body able to reach a seat, and no later claim that eating meant assent. Unity purchased with unpaid labor or a dish somebody cannot eat is poor bookkeeping and worse hospitality.

Pella can shrink the feast, split courses and tables, mark abstentions, move the grievance interval, credit substitutions, and salvage a postponed day. She will not roast “probably,” seat rank above hearing or access, hold a hot course through an endless ceremonial quarrel, or let a gift enter the rite before its receiver knows its proposed office.

Pella speaks in kitchen arithmetic:

> “Give me names or give me empty benches. I cannot roast ‘probably.’”

> “A tradition with no steward is a wish. A wish does not keep soup warm.”

> “You may disagree at my table. You may not make the kitchen pretend you agreed.”

## The seven baskets

Use the baskets in any order; carry unsettled ones elsewhere. A decision is complete only when the table can name the affected people, the promised act, its steward, and what happens when the plan changes.

### First basket: names and numbers

The two family lists do not count guests the same way. The Vale list names households, assuming spouses and dependent children are included. The river list names people with standing, assuming that anyone currently carrying a shared duty may accompany them. Pella has thirty-eight certain guests, seven probable guests, and nine people whom one list treats as included while the other does not.

Do not solve this by choosing one counting custom. Build a named register. Each entry should distinguish:

- invited person;
- accompanying person or dependent;
- feast attendance;
- ceremony attendance;
- lodging needed;
- access or comfort requirement;
- food choice or abstention;
- gift or grievance role; and
- the person who confirmed the entry.

Several guests expose the danger of representative categories.

- **Agnes Vale** needs a stable chair away from grinding noise and a clear view of anyone addressing her. She does not need to be carried, seated at the ceremonial “head,” or treated as representative of mortal age.
- **Deep-Reed**, Serein’s elder cousin, cannot crouch on willow roots. She wants a backed chair on dry matting with her bare feet in a shallow moving basin. She does not want a submerged seat.
- **Noll Ferry**, a river-born boatman with an old lung injury, sleeps best in a dry shrine room and dislikes damp bedding. Assigning every river guest beneath the willows would make him ill.
- **Lilt-before-Storm**, a young current-reader, can sleep almost anywhere but wakes in panic if she cannot hear running water. A cot beside the market fountain suits her better than an honored dry chamber.
- **Aunt Sal Vale** can walk the willow platforms and is secretly eager to do so, but she wants a handrail and will deny needing it if the request is made publicly.
- Three children from the river household and two mill apprentices want to sleep in the same loft because they are building lantern boats. Their guardians must agree; the children’s enthusiasm is not sufficient authority.

A completed register may reduce the guest list, add labor, or reveal that a modest accommodation solves an apparent cultural divide. A guest may attend the ceremony but not the feast, sleep elsewhere, bring their own food, or abstain from one custom without withdrawing from the marriage.

### Second basket: food and source

The taking ledger matters more than the ingredient category. River households eat fish, grain, greens, shellfish, fruit, and meat according to source, season, obligation, and personal preference. Mortal guests are equally varied. The protected trout are wrong because of the closed reach, not because river folk never eat fish.

Pella can build a credible feast from available stores:

1. **Arrival cups and road bread.** Barley water, mint, salt, and small wheat rolls are served before the formal feast. They are hospitality for travelers, not the first shared course, so nobody must wait hungry through the grievance interval.
2. **Common-reach mussels or herb broth.** Serein’s ledger permits a limited mussel taking from the lower common reach. Guests may choose the broth without shellfish. The gatherers are named and credited.
3. **Jory Salt’s sea catch.** **Jory Salt** has smoked silver hake from a licensed coastal crew. It is acceptable to many guests, but it is not an ethically pure substitute that appeared without labor. Jory wants his crew, transport, salt, and price named.
4. **Mill grain and garden dishes.** Vale flour, onion cakes, braised roots, river beans from planted beds, and greens cut above the flood mark can feed the majority of guests without pretending to be neutral symbols.
5. **Honey, fruit, and reed sugar.** The final sweet course can be assembled cold if ceremony or grievances delay the schedule.

Pella has oven and labor limits. She can serve forty-two people one hot course at once. She can feed up to fifty if the meal uses two seatings, one hot and one cold course, or extra cooks. Every added ceremonial pause threatens a particular dish, not “the feast” in the abstract.

Jory is brisk, proud, and unimpressed by moral theater. He can expand his order if paid and if two people help clean and portion the fish. He will not accept public thanks that call his goods “the safe kind” while omitting the crew who caught them. If the witnesses approach him as a last-minute instrument of reconciliation, he says, “I sell supper. I do not sell innocence.”

For each course, name who grew, gathered, caught, traded, cooked, or released it, and what obligation follows. Pella may speak the credit, print it on small cards, or enter it in the witness record. Provenance is part of the meal: it keeps a gift from concealing a closed reach, unpaid labor, or a debt the couple never accepted.

Pella will print two notes beside the same dishes if one grand title would lie. One can name river permissions, returned obligations, and keepers; the other can name mill grain, paid labor, and household gifts. The meal need not pretend the two accounts are one account in order to feed everyone at one table.

Her cash box follows the same discipline. The mill's grain account, Tomas's personal purse, and the household wedding fund hang from separate hooks. Each has a different signer and a different remedy when it runs short. Pella will spend from an authorized purse; she will not let a wedding invoice become evidence that the marriage acquired the mill, its debts, or its lease.

### Third basket: labor and time

The wedding has more willing hands than coordinated shifts. Tomas has promised wheel coverage, platform lifting, and evening kitchen work. Neris has promised current checks, guest guidance, and source verification. If both keep every promise, neither reaches the private consent rehearsal rested.

Pella asks the witnesses to identify every task that presently depends on one of the couple:

- returning the trout;
- confirming river sources;
- moving benches;
- collecting borrowed cups;
- escorting guests over wet ground;
- supervising children near the fountain;
- carrying grievance stones;
- translating names and announcements; and
- checking the final guest count.

Most tasks can be reassigned. Mara can release two mill hands after the afternoon grind. Orren can lead platform lifting. Rain-at-Noon can verify source marks. Mera can maintain the guest register. Brin can confirm individual guest needs under supervision. Aunt Sal can collect cups and discover that practical service grants more influence than claiming precedence.

Make labor visible. Each promise should have a named worker, start time, replacement, and stopping point. Volunteers may refuse new work. The witnesses’ authority to ask questions does not make the party an unlimited labor pool, although adventurers may earn considerable goodwill by taking one difficult shift themselves.

### Fourth basket: seats, access, and table order

The existing market hall seats thirty on dry benches. Twelve additional places can be made along the fountain with removable boards and shallow water trays. Dessa can build more, but every added place costs reed panels needed for the ceremony.

The Vales imagine a head table with Agnes and the couple at its center. The river household imagines people seated by current obligation, with the person owed a duty facing the person who owes it. Neither arrangement accommodates everyone.

Pella offers several workable plans:

- **The hinge table:** Tomas and Neris sit where two long tables meet. Agnes and Serein have equal sight lines without being forced beside one another.
- **The open square:** four short tables leave the fountain visible in the center. Guests can face grievance speakers without establishing one head.
- **Two first courses, one final table:** households eat their first course in familiar groupings, then join for gifts and sweets. This preserves comfort but makes unity a later act rather than an assumed starting state.
- **Named mixed tables:** people sit near those whose needs or duties they actually share—workers near water readers, children near guardians, gift givers near consenting receivers—rather than alternating mortal and river bodies for appearance.

No elder is owed an unsafe seat. No relative is entitled to sit beside the couple merely because a family diagram puts them there. The couple may reserve seats for witnesses, musicians, stewards, and absent people whose names they wish acknowledged.

Pella's lifting rota is as particular as the seating plan. One worker steadies Deep-Reed's chair, one keeps the shallow basin flowing, and one named relief takes over before the first hot course. If any name disappears, the duty becomes open again; it does not fall automatically to 'the river household' or to whichever Vale happens to be nearest.

**Aunt Sal Vale** is delighted by every river custom until she learns that her preferred “aunt’s place” may disappear. She is sociable, observant, and capable of useful work, but she uses charm to turn assumptions into faits accomplis. She can concede any table shape if Agnes remains visible and if her own service is publicly recognized. She will not accept being told that mortal kinship is vulgar or that only river obligations deserve ceremonial placement.

### Fifth basket: lodging

Cresswater can house the invited guests, but not by sorting them into “river” and “mortal” quarters.

Available spaces include:

- eight dry cots in the mill’s cleaned eastern loft;
- six quiet beds at the shrine, two accessible without stairs;
- ten market-stall cots under weatherproof awnings near the fountain;
- eight willow-platform sleeping places with moving water below;
- four places in the ferry shed, dry but noisy at dawn; and
- household floors and spare rooms offered by named neighbors.

Assign lodging through the register. Deep-Reed needs a level route and a basin, which Dessa can provide at the market stalls. Noll Ferry needs a dry shrine bed. Lilt-before-Storm needs audible water, not a wet mattress. Agnes sleeps at home. Aunt Sal wants the adventure of a willow platform but requires a rail and a guide. The children’s shared loft requires Mara, Orren, and the assigned night guardian to agree.

Lodging creates labor: bedding must be carried, platforms checked, lamps supplied, and guests guided after dark. A promise of “both households will find room” is not complete until specific hosts accept specific guests.

### Sixth basket: gifts and declared intentions

Pella has put a red cord around the gift basket because five objects have already acquired meanings their givers did not intend.

- Agnes’s veil offers lineage and remembrance but signifies concealed breath if placed over Neris’s face.
- Orren’s closed iron ring offers durable family labor but signifies captivity without outlet.
- Mara’s commissioned handstone, cut from a retired millstone, offers steadiness and provision but can imply that Neris’s course should be fixed.
- Aunt Sal’s red cradle ribbon offers hoped-for descendants but publicly presumes children the couple has not promised.
- Jory’s cedar salt box offers preserved food and safe roads. One river cousin assumes salt means water made barren; Jory means that the couple should never be stranded without stores.

Do not adjudicate symbols as though objects have one secret correct meaning. Use a declared-gift procedure:

1. The giver names the material, maker, source, intended honor, and any duty attached.
2. The receiver paraphrases what they believe they are being offered.
3. The receiver may accept it as made, accept a transformed use, defer it, receive it privately, or refuse it.
4. Any transformation preserves the maker’s credit and states who may alter the object.
5. No surprise gift enters the public ceremony unless both Tomas and Neris accept the surprise itself.

The veil, ring, and handstone can travel to the mill, willows, yard, shrine, or rehearsal for testing. The cradle ribbon may become a cord around the compact chest, remain a private hope, or be withheld. The salt box may be paired with a water bowl and presented as stores for travel between homes. A refused gift is not automatically an insult. A giver may withdraw it rather than let the object say something false.

Orren has left Pella an invoice and two iron samples: the closed ring he first imagined and an open spiral fastened with replaceable rush. The second keeps the hammerwork visible, costs less to maintain, and can be removed without cutting iron from the wearer. The samples do not decide Neris's answer. They make the available answers concrete enough to compare.

### Seventh basket: grievances, abstentions, and the order of eating

River custom requires unresolved obligations to be named before shared food pretends that everyone is at peace. Mortal guests fear that the wedding feast will become a public accusation. Both concerns are reasonable.

Pella, Rain-at-Noon, and Mera can operate a bounded procedure.

#### Before the feast

- Guests receive arrival cups and road bread so nobody negotiates while hungry.
- Proposed grievances are submitted to Rain and Mera by noon.
- Each entry names speaker, respondent, duty, requested next act, steward, and later hearing date if needed.
- The stewards reject character attacks, claims over the couple, surprise testimony, and matters too complex to understand in one breath.
- The old flood is assigned to its separate hearing unless Agnes and Serein both request a narrowly stated public obligation.

Pella keeps two flood-year market records in the grievance packet. The delivery slate marks two river signs before the mill bell. A separate wage slate pays a porter to carry the first warning to the mill gate, but its receipt line is blank. Together they prove dispatch and route, not delivery, acknowledgment, escalation, or what Perrin chose after the water reached him.

#### The public interval

- Pella sets twelve minutes and no more than four public entries.
- Rain states the scope: unfinished obligation, not verdict on a person.
- The speaker names the duty and requested next act in one breath.
- The respondent may acknowledge it, state that it was discharged, contest it while accepting a hearing, or decline a public reply and accept private stewardship.
- The steward places the marked obligation stone in a water bowl. Washing the stone means the matter has been honestly carried into the meal, not resolved.
- When time ends, unresolved entries remain in the ledger and the first shared course begins.

Private entries remain valid. A guest may attend while abstaining from the grievance interval, one course, a toast, a dance, or a gift. Pella marks abstention with a blank reed token at the guest’s place. The token says only “present, not participating in this act.” It is not a vote against the marriage.

The limit protects Rain from a feast that lies about unfinished duties, Agnes from an ambush over Perrin's death, and Pella from holding supper for a quarrel without an end.

## Brin Quickwater and accountable comedy

**Brin Quickwater** is Neris’s cousin, a charming idler with a gift for delivering inventions in the tone of an archivist. He has claimed that river guests eat only fish, that odd-numbered cups invite drought, and that a groom must be addressed by the first object he drops. He does not intend harm. He expects adults to recognize play and is genuinely startled when Pella orders twelve trout.

Brin is no saboteur. Charge the joke to him. He returns fish, carries the guest slate, and confirms each river guest's actual needs. Under Pella's eye he becomes a surprisingly good interviewer, because nobody wants him answering on their behalf.

If confronted cruelly, Brin retreats into mockery. If given accountable work, he admits, “I thought the lie was too decorated to stand.” Pella answers, “Then next time decorate the truth and carry the basket.”

Brin can later serve as a useful master of abstention tokens or children’s lanterns. His comedy should reveal the danger of assumptions without making river custom itself ridiculous.

## Market complications

For pressure, choose one or two complications rooted in appetite, labor, or a bad inference. Do not import whimsy from nowhere.

1. **The leaking trout tank.** Water loss, crowding, and the cracked cart wheel force immediate action before discussion.
2. **Nine uncounted companions.** The family lists include people differently. The witnesses must confirm invitations instead of announcing a universal counting rule.
3. **The cold onion cakes.** A ceremonial meeting overruns the oven schedule. Pella asks which course changes, who eats later, or who leaves the meeting to help.
4. **The honorable wrong bed.** Deep-Reed is assigned a prestigious willow niche she cannot reach, while Noll Ferry receives a damp riverside cot he cannot safely use.
5. **The head-seat dispute.** Aunt Sal and a river duty-holder both expect the same sight line for different reasons. Rebuilding the table or clarifying function solves more than declaring rank.
6. **The surprise cradle ribbon.** Aunt Sal plans to tie it around Neris during the feast. Neris may accept another use, receive it privately, or refuse it. Stop the surprise before a crowd can turn refusal into spectacle.
7. **The borrowed cups.** Half the cups belong to people who must leave before cleanup. Reassigning washing labor becomes a test of whether gratitude includes practical return.

## Productive scenes

- The party returns the protected trout through a crowded market while keeping them alive.
- Pella makes each witness replace a category on the guest list with three named people and their actual needs.
- Jory refuses to become an anonymous “safe substitute” and negotiates public credit and extra hands.
- Deep-Reed and Noll Ferry exchange their assigned lodgings and expose why the original sorting failed.
- Aunt Sal bargains for recognition by accepting cup collection or guest guidance as a real office.
- Brin confirms preferences under Pella’s eye and discovers that accurate answers can be funnier than inventions.
- A trial gift declaration lets Agnes, Orren, Mara, or Jory hear how the receiver understands the object.
- Rain demonstrates the bounded grievance procedure with the broken market-basket debt she owes Agnes.
- Pella lays out recoverable, perishable, committed, and lost stores so postponement can be discussed honestly.

## Decisions that travel forward

Record at least the following before leaving the market:

- confirmed and uncertain guest counts;
- named access and lodging assignments;
- menu courses, sources, abstentions, and labor;
- table form and the seats whose placement serves a specific function;
- the grievance stewards, submission deadline, public limit, and later hearings;
- each gift’s status: accepted, transformed, private, deferred, or refused;
- unresolved work and the person who must answer it; and
- recoverable versus irrecoverable costs if the wedding is postponed.

These decisions should become visible at the rehearsal and wedding. A guest who was not confirmed may arrive late or stay away. A promised handrail must exist. A source should be named when the dish is served. An abstention token should remain visible. A transformed gift should carry both the giver’s intention and the receiver’s stated limit.

## Connections

The market points naturally toward every other preparation.

- Return to the **House of Open Measure** to enter confirmed guests, gift meanings, abstentions, and unresolved duties in the compact appendices.
- Visit **Vale Mill and Hearth** or the **House Beneath the Willows** to confirm invitations, labor releases, and named accommodations.
- Bring vows, grievance limits, or disputed gift language to the **Shrine of the Open Door**.
- Bring seating, basins, handrails, and lodging platforms to the **Reedwright’s Yard**.
- Bring course timing and public grievance intervals to the **Bridge of Three Tunes** so the musicians know what they must cover.
- Bring the old delivery slate and final headcount to the **Flood Meadow and Old Ford** for rehearsal.

## If the market is skipped or reached late

A wedding can proceed without a full feast. It cannot honestly pretend that unasked guests were accommodated or that uncertain food was responsibly sourced. Use only stores whose source, labor, and safety are known. Reduce the guest-facing meal before guessing at appetites. A simple bread, orchard, cheese, and sea-catch table is better than a symbolic menu built from protected trout or unnamed labor.

Undeclared gifts remain private or withheld. The public grievance interval occurs only if speakers, respondents, duties, stewards, and later hearings were prepared. Otherwise, Pella begins the meal at the fixed cue and directs unfinished obligations to private hearings. Nobody is surprised into public testimony.

Late market corrections reduce scale rather than rewrite consent. A guest may change attendance, seating, lodging, food, gift, dance, or grievance participation. Update that named person's entry. Do not treat one river guest's answer as representative of the river household or one Vale relative's answer as binding the mill table.

## Failure forward

The feast may become smaller, split, delayed, or less symmetrical. Some guests may lodge apart. A course may be omitted. A gift may be withheld. A grievance may move to private hearing. A guest may remain present while abstaining. None of these outcomes invalidates the marriage.

Hospitality goes false when it keeps speaking in collective nouns after particular people have answered. Carry the damage forward at human scale: cold food, an inaccessible seat, an offended giver, unpaid labor, a missing guest, or a public correction at the wedding. The repair is the same each time—name the person, the authority, and the revisable promise.

Maintains the named guest register and helps keep attendance, food, lodging, gifts, and assent separate.
Her attendance, gift, and household precedence must remain separate from other forms of assent.
Controls named mill labor, shared-loft approval, and the handstone declaration without turning hospitality or gifts into household-wide assent.

encounters.title: The Doorless Shrine
encounters.summary: Keeper Ansel clears the rite down to six acts, then tests every vow, name, exchange, and open clause in words Tomas and Neris can repeat.
encounters.opening_view: Keeper Ansel has removed almost everything people call a wedding. No altar, no procession, no place of honor: only six wooden blocks laid across the bare floor—consent, household, names, exchange, promises, departure. Fourteen old compacts cover the benches, including one that ends in refusal. On a side shelf, a veil, a ring, and other returned gifts wait without shame. Ansel touches none of them. “Begin,” he says, “with what each person may still decline.”
encounters.content:
## Situation
The Doorless Shrine has no wall on its river side and no door on its road side. Fourteen compact tablets cover the benches: marriages, adoptions, burial agreements, ferry partnerships, one refusal, and several settlements whose open clauses outlived the people who first signed them. Keeper Ansel Rook has removed the ceremonial objects from the floor and set down six plain wooden blocks.

Each block names an act the witnesses may later certify: **consent, household standing, names, exchange, promises, departure**. Everything else must earn its place by helping Tomas and Neris perform one of those acts without changing it behind their backs. A veil may shelter or mourn. A ring may promise or bind. A boat may receive or remove. A crowd response may recognize a name or manufacture one. Ansel will not let inherited beauty answer those questions by momentum.

The work here is spoken and repeatable. Tomas and Neris choose the order, the words, the silences, and any reserved matter. Each poetic promise must survive an ordinary paraphrase. Each name must identify the person without forcing symmetry. Each object must be offered with a declared office and accepted in that office. If one block cannot yet be crossed, red cord marks the open line; the rest of the ceremony need not pretend the cord is absent.

## Keeper Ansel Rook
Ansel is narrow and weathered, with a voice that carries without force. He keeps compact tablets, marries across customs, and buries strangers whose households dispute the body. Any sentence that wins applause before explanation makes him wary.

He speaks in verbs: enter, retain, answer, warn, care, return, leave, revise. Metaphor is welcome after its duty survives plain speech. Ansel will rearrange the six acts, use one vow or many, keep parallel household descriptions, link stable identity to changing names, transform or omit gifts, mark an open clause, move the site, or let another officiate.

He will not accept a relative's answer for a principal, a name invented for symmetry, a future child assigned as ceremonial property, a surprise duty, compelled truth, or a record strengthened by fatigue and silence.

Ansel's sentences are plain enough to remember:

> “A vow may be beautiful after it has survived being ordinary.”

> “Do not promise forever until you can tell me what you owe next winter.”

> “The record is allowed an open door. That is what doors are for.”

## The six ceremonial functions

The six markers are an audit, not six mandatory speeches. Several functions may share one act; one function may require several. A sequence is ready when the table can say what an observer sees and what Tomas and Neris say it means.

### 1. Consent

The ceremony needs a public choice that follows, rather than replaces, the House of Open Measure’s private consent procedure. Ansel asks each person three short questions:

1. Do you choose this marriage now?
2. Do you choose the duties entered in the witness record?
3. Is any stated matter provisional, refused, or reserved for later hearing?

Tomas and Neris answer separately, without completing one another’s sentences. They need not disclose private reasons. “Not yet” is a valid answer. “Yes, except for the child-standing clause reserved to later hearing” is more certifiable than an exhausted unqualified yes.

If either person changes an answer from the House interviews, pause. Mera records the change; Ansel asks whether new language is needed; the other partner paraphrases the revised term; and the ceremony resumes, moves the disputed function later, or postpones. Guests may be disappointed. Disappointment is not coercive authority.

### 2. Household standing

The public act must show what is entered, retained, or created without pretending that household has one uncontested definition. Ansel offers three workable forms.

- **One household, two dwellings.** Tomas and Neris name the eastern rooms and the willow house as homes of one marriage, then state the duties that apply in each place.
- **Two continuing households joined.** Each retains standing in their present household and accepts defined duties toward the other, while the eastern rooms become a shared dwelling rather than a new corporate household.
- **A new household of the open reach.** The couple names a third marital household whose members retain Vale and river standing. It is elegant only if they want the third standing and accept the extra record work; conciliation alone is no reason to create it.

The ceremony does not need to settle the couple’s preferred description if every consequence is explicit. It does need to state keys, return, warning, care, domestic authority, adoption duties, and retained kinship. Ansel tests any formula by asking, “Who may return at midnight without permission?” and “Who answers a spawning closure when Neris is upriver?”

### 3. Names

The shrine registry uses four separate lines:

- **stable witness identity**, tied to a mark, parentage, and prior records;
- **current answered name**, spoken at the ceremony;
- **recognized bynames**, appended in sequence rather than overwritten;
- **dwellings and household standing**, recorded without turning residence into a surname.

Neris presently chooses **Neris Reed-in-Rain**. Her stable witness identity links her to Serein-at-Alderfall, the House Beneath the Willows, and her earlier child-name, Small-Reed-After-Thunder. A later byname may be appended if she accepts it. The earlier names remain searchable and do not become names guests may use against her preference.

Tomas remains **Tomas Vale**. He may be described as adopted to the House Beneath the Willows if he accepts that standing. He does not need a river byname, and Ansel will not invent one to make the folio appear balanced. If the river household later gives him a byname through ordinary relationship, the House can append it with Tomas’s consent.

A person announcing the couple should use the names they currently answer. The written record may be more extensive than the public announcement. Guests who cannot pronounce a byname can rehearse it, ask permission for an accepted short form, or remain silent at the naming response. Difficulty is not license to replace a name.

### 4. Exchange

An exchange can be an object, an act, a shared use, or no material gift. The minimum procedure is exact:

1. The giver states source, maker, intended honor, and attached duty.
2. The receiver states what they understand themselves to be accepting.
3. The receiver accepts, transforms, defers, receives privately, or refuses.
4. The witnesses state any alteration that changes the object’s public meaning.

The veil might become a canopy under which both stand, a wrapping around the compact chest, or a cloth held behind the couple while the dead are named. The iron ring might become an open spiral, two matching clasps, or a fitting in the threshold bridge. Mara’s handstone might support the shared water bowl or rest on a table that moves between homes. The boat can serve the household-standing function rather than the exchange function. No object must carry more meanings than the people handling it can explain.

Ansel has a basket of blank wooden counters for a useful rehearsal. Each giver places a counter where the object will be used and speaks the intended sentence without displaying the object. Tomas and Neris then paraphrase. If the sentence fails, nobody has yet been pressured by family attention or craft expense.

Beside the counters lies Ansel's return-shelf register. It records a veil accepted as a canopy, a cup returned unopened, and a household token received in private. None of those marriages failed because the exchange changed or stopped. The register keeps three separate lines—what the giver meant, what the receiver accepted, and what finally happened to the object—so later readers cannot turn courtesy into consent.

### 5. Promises

Promises should name continuing duties, limits, revision, and release. Ansel distinguishes four things that “while this river runs” presently collapses:

- **continuing obligation:** a duty owed without seasonal renewal;
- **renewed obligation:** a duty reviewed at a named interval or changed condition;
- **interrupted obligation:** a duty paused by absence, incapacity, danger, or conflicting stewardship;
- **released obligation:** a duty ended through separation, replacement, discharge, or mutual revision.

The couple can choose one of several vow structures.

#### Plain paired vows

Each names the other, the chosen marriage, the dwellings or households recognized, the principal care and warning duties accepted, and the right to reopen terms when circumstances change. This is the clearest form and the easiest for guests to hear.

#### Image followed by plain speech

The poetic line is spoken first, then translated by the speaker. Tomas might say that he will keep faith “while wheel and water answer one another,” then add that he means he will not ignore Neris’s warnings, conceal mill decisions affecting the channel, or treat changed residence as abandonment. Neris might promise “through every honest course,” then state that she means returning, communicating absence, sharing care, and revising duties rather than disappearing into a new current.

#### Separate duty vows

The couple makes shorter promises at the relevant acts: care at the veil or canopy, bounded adoption at the boat, mutual warning at the water bowl, residence at the keys, and endurance at the final joining. This prevents one speech from becoming an unreadable contract but may lengthen the ceremony.

#### Compact affirmation

Mera reads a concise summary of the recorded terms. Each partner affirms that summary and may add one personal promise outside the legal record. This works well in rain or when long public speech would exclude guests, but the summary must still be available for paraphrase beforehand.

None of these structures needs a detailed separation ceremony at the wedding. The record should nevertheless name the right to request revision, the stewards for a future hearing, immediate care and property protections during separation, and the fact that ending a marriage does not make the original choice fraudulent.

### 6. Departure

Departure shows that the couple leaves the ceremony together by present choice. It decides no permanent residence. Stage the route so it does not contradict the household terms.

Possible forms include:

- Tomas enters the threshold boat, Neris receives him into river kinship, and both leave the boat over the shared bridge toward the eastern rooms;
- the couple approaches from separate banks, joins at the runnel, and leaves along the mill path before returning later to the willows;
- the couple begins together beneath the veil canopy, completes the six functions, and departs by the old ford carrying the compact chest between them; or
- in severe rain, they cross the shrine threshold together, touch water and dry stone, and leave through the open side while the musicians carry the joining tune outdoors.

The departure must be possible for the actual bodies, weather, and site. A symbolic route that requires Neris to stand away from moving water too long or Tomas to enter unsafe depth is not more sacred for being difficult.

## The tablet archive

Ansel’s records provide precedents without supplying a hidden correct answer. Choose two or three tablets according to the party’s questions.

### Alder-Sill compact

A ferryman and a carpenter retained separate households for thirty-one years. Their compact named one shared bedroom above the ferry office, two separate property books, reciprocal rescue duties, and an annual winter review. The record calls them “one marriage across two houses” without deciding whether that phrase created a third household. The marriage endured because its practical terms could be revised without relitigating affection.

### Greybank compact

A mill widow promised to receive “all that comes to my spouse’s door.” She meant kin and guests. Her spouse’s road household understood debts, fugitives, and sworn dependents. Both paraphrased the line differently after the ceremony, and neither had been asked beforehand. The marriage did not fail immediately, but the phrase caused years of contested liability. Ansel uses the tablet to show why poetry must be tested against inconvenient examples.

### Reed-and-Candle compact

Two partners agreed on residence, care, names, and exchange but could not agree whether an adopted child would enter one inheritance line. They married with the issue reserved to a mixed hearing after the child’s seventh year, if the child existed and if the affected child wished the question heard. No child was born. The open clause harmed nobody and prevented a hypothetical person from being assigned for the sake of a complete-looking tablet.

### Stonewake refusal

A groom repeated every family-approved answer but could not describe the household duties in private without looking to his elder brother. The witnesses postponed certification. The couple married six months later under shorter terms after the groom had taken separate lodging and negotiated without his brother present. The tablet records the first refusal and the later marriage without shame.

## Vow workshop

Run the workshop as comparison rather than composition by committee.

1. Tomas and Neris each bring one sentence they want to keep.
2. The other partner paraphrases the sentence and names any feared consequence.
3. Ansel supplies one inconvenient case: flood, absence, illness, changed work, separation, or a new byname.
4. The speaker revises, narrows, divides, or keeps the sentence with an explanatory line.
5. Mera marks whether the result is record language, ceremony language, personal promise, or unresolved hope.

Family members may explain what a phrase means in their own custom. They may not negotiate the couple’s answer while either partner is absent. The adventurers can propose alternatives, ask consequences, compare precedents, and protect time for private consultation.

No perfect vow is required. Tomas and Neris must know which words create duties, which express hope, and which hopes remain outside the compact.

## Ceremony orders

Leave the shrine with one primary order and one weather-shortened order.

### The meeting order

- separate approaches;
- public consent;
- names;
- household standing and boat threshold;
- declared exchanges;
- promises;
- grievance acknowledgment if used;
- joining tune and shared departure.

This order makes difference visible before joining. It requires more space and two legible approach routes.

### The compact-first order

- couple enters together;
- public consent;
- Mera’s concise compact summary;
- household and name affirmations;
- exchanges;
- personal promises;
- departure.

This order is shorter and adapts well to rain. It can feel overly administrative unless music, objects, and family roles remain personal.

### The threshold order

- both households gather on their chosen footing;
- Tomas enters the boat and is received;
- Neris crosses beneath the Vale canopy or accepts another lineage act;
- both state retained standing and names;
- promises and exchange occur at the shared threshold;
- both leave by a route belonging to neither household alone.

This order gives family acts strong visibility. It should be used only if Tomas and Neris accept the sequence and no gift becomes a condition of marriage.

## Shrine complications

If the workshop floats free of the wedding, introduce one complication:

1. **The applauded sentence.** A family member hears one draft line and begins repeating it through town before the couple accepts it. The witnesses must correct the rumor without publicly humiliating the source.
2. **The symmetrical folio.** A junior copyist has prepared matching surname and byname spaces. Neris objects to the replacement surname; Tomas objects to a ceremonial river name invented for him. The form, not the people, must change.
3. **The wrong precedent.** Aunt Sal finds the Greybank tablet’s opening blessing and cites it as proof that the whole compact succeeded. Reading the reverse exposes the liability dispute.
4. **The private promise.** Tomas or Neris offers a beautiful personal line that the other loves but does not want entered as enforceable duty. Ansel helps preserve it outside the compact.
5. **The impossible pronunciation.** A well-meaning announcer cannot manage Reed-in-Rain under pressure. Neris decides whether to coach, authorize a short form, appoint another announcer, or omit the congregational response.
6. **The missing marker.** A child carries away one of the six wooden markers. The party must identify which function has vanished from the current plan rather than merely replacing the block.

## Decisions that travel forward

Record at least:

- Tomas’s and Neris’s ceremony names and registry treatment;
- the public consent questions and any reserved matter;
- the chosen household-standing language or preserved descriptive disagreement;
- the exchange status and declared meaning of every public object;
- the vow structure and ordinary-language paraphrases;
- the primary and shortened ceremony orders;
- the chosen departure act;
- who speaks, reads, announces, witnesses, and stewards any open clause; and
- what event requires a pause rather than improvisation.

Take the order to the Reedwright’s Yard for spatial design and to the Bridge of Three Tunes for cues. Return any changed term to the House of Open Measure before the ceremony.

## Connections

- Return to the **House of Open Measure** for private reconfirmation and final entry of names, duties, and open clauses.
- Visit **Vale Mill and Hearth** and the **House Beneath the Willows** to test family acts without allowing family recognition to become a condition of consent.
- Bring guest roles, grievance timing, and object declarations from the **Market of Seven Baskets**.
- Bring the six-function order and primary site assumptions to the **Reedwright’s Yard**.
- Bring speaking lengths, responses, and joining points to the **Bridge of Three Tunes**.
- Test both full and shortened orders at the **Flood Meadow and Old Ford**.

## If the shrine is skipped or reached late

The six functions do not belong to the shrine. Mera or another competent reader can conduct them in ordinary language: separate and public consent, accepted household standing, current names, declared exchange, paraphrasable promises, and chosen departure. Use no poetic sentence that either principal cannot explain. No object completes a function by appearing.

Without Ansel and the archive, the witnesses should make fewer claims about precedent and use a plainer record. They may preserve an open clause without citing an earlier compact. Neris's name chain remains possible because the House can record stable identity and current answered name; the shrine is useful corroboration, not exclusive authority.

If a late archive tablet or officiant's concern changes a material term, reopen only that term. A precedent may offer a better form but cannot overrule the principals. Ansel may decline wording he cannot intelligibly read or archive; the ceremony can continue without shrine officiation, and the record should say so.

## Failure forward

Ansel may reject one vow, one name entry, or one public act while accepting the rest. The couple may use fewer promises, remove an object, reserve a clause, change the ceremony order, choose a private exchange, postpone, or proceed without his officiation.

Do not treat simplification as failure. Failure occurs when a beautiful form conceals a duty or when public momentum substitutes for present choice. Even then, the remedy is a pause, a narrower statement, a visible boundary, or honest refusal—not a revelation that the couple unknowingly violated an ancient taboo.

encounters.title: The Reedwright's Yard
encounters.summary: Dessa Reedwright prices the metaphors: safe footing, clean water return, visible stations, named labor, and a fallback ready before the rain decides for them.
encounters.opening_view: Dessa Reedwright has put Agnes Vale’s chair on a floating panel and ordered three apprentices to walk across it. The panel rolls. The apprentices catch the chair. Around them, fish gates lean against planks, a ceremonial boat is tied sideways, and four handsome plans flap beneath a board painted METAPHORS, UNPRICED. Dessa draws her measuring cord through the mud, looks from the chair to the witnesses, and asks the only question she considers fit for poetry: “What, exactly, is meant to carry her?”
encounters.content:
## Situation
The **Reedwright's Yard** occupies a shelf of packed clay below the market bridge. Fish gates lean against plank stacks. Reed panels float in troughs while apprentices jump on them one at a time. A small ceremonial boat is tied sideways between two posts. Four sketches for “one place for both households” flap beneath Dessa's painted judgment: **METAPHORS, UNPRICED**.

One sketch puts every river guest in ankle-deep water. One lifts the Vales onto a dais Agnes cannot hear from. One sends Tomas away in the boat. The last draws a beautiful spiral with no opening wide enough for Deep-Reed's chair. Dessa Reedwright can build any meaning the couple chooses, provided somebody tells her its weight, route, capacity, labor, and return.

Bring Dessa the shrine's six acts and the market's named guests. She turns them into wet and dry footing, sight lines, handrails, rill intake, clean return, a stationary threshold, work lanes, musician positions, and a stripped fallback. The site works when every needed person can see or hear the act that concerns them, no one must risk injury to prove trust, and rain can move the ceremony without changing who receives whom.

Lumber cannot reconcile a family. Reeds cannot decide where home is. They can, however, expose a false answer before fifty guests stand on it.

## Dessa Reedwright
Dessa is compact, sun-browned, and missing the tip of one finger to a winter lashing. She tests a platform by standing on it while somebody else shakes the frame. Custom earns her respect when it admits weight, depth, distance, labor, and bodies. Ask lumber to settle an unspoken quarrel and she writes **METAPHOR** where another builder would write a price.

She wants one modular build that can move among meadow, wheel yard, ford, and shrine rise. She also wants twelve workers named where other people would write “the river provided.”

Dessa accepts asymmetry, linked platforms, separate routes, ordinary handrails, a stationary boat, smaller scale, and decoration cut for access or fallback. She refuses stagnant display water, risk called trust, chairs treated as blemishes, untested capacity, blocked work lanes, and metaphor changes delivered after the last peg is driven.

Dessa prices speech as readily as timber:

> “Tell me what the bridge means after you tell me who crosses it.”

> “Water may be sacred. It is still heavy.”

> “I can build one place. I cannot build one consequence from four promises.”

## The yard inventory

Dessa has enough material for one full site and one stripped fallback, not two elaborate sites.

- eighteen woven reed mats, each safe for four standing adults or two chairs;
- twelve dry plank sections, each six feet long;
- six shallow rill trays with pegged couplings;
- four low bridge sections with handrail sockets;
- two backed basin chairs, one already promised to Deep-Reed;
- eight removable handrail posts;
- one open threshold boat;
- two broad turning platforms suitable for chairs, musicians, or exchange tables;
- sixteen lantern stakes;
- one compact chest stand;
- three water-return screens to keep flowers, wax, food, and dropped objects out of the channel; and
- enough spare reed and cord for repair, not for an unplanned second grand aisle.

A crew of eight can erect the meadow design in four hours on dry ground. Moving it to the mill yard takes two hours if the modules are labeled and the route remains clear. Moving it to the shrine rise takes three because the rill water must be lifted from the runnel and returned downhill. The willow-bank design requires less material but admits fewer dry chairs. The old ford can be made usable quickly, but guests will stand in separated groups and the ceremony must be shorter.

These limits create decisions rather than punishment. Decorative arches, extra lanterns, and matched railings consume the same labor needed for a dry turning space or fallback labeling.

## The site survey

Dessa asks the party to choose a primary site only after walking all four candidates with the guest register and six-function order.

### Flood meadow

**Capacity:** up to fifty seated or sixty standing in fair weather.

**Strengths:** broad sight lines, room for two approaches, space for tables and musicians, easy access from market and mill, and enough open sky for the joining light.

**Weaknesses:** overnight rills appear unpredictably; ground softens under chairs; shade is limited; the exact ford edge changes; and every long route becomes harder for Agnes, Deep-Reed, and small children.

**Best use:** paired household areas joined by a central threshold, with modular rills crossing raised mats. The meadow makes the whole wedding visible but needs the strongest rain plan.

### Old wheel yard

**Capacity:** forty-two seated if one mill access lane remains open; forty-eight with some guests standing.

**Strengths:** existing stone runnel, dry packed ground, nearby eastern rooms, kitchen access, familiar mortal acoustics, and a visible wheel for the joining light.

**Weaknesses:** grinding noise, work traffic, narrow western entrance, risk that river guests appear merely accommodated inside Vale property, and no room for two long processions.

**Best use:** compact-first or threshold order. The eastern runnel can feed shallow rills and return water without pumps. Ask Neris what would make the yard a shared site instead of the mill receiving her household as visitors.

### Willow bank

**Capacity:** thirty-six comfortable witnesses, fewer if many dry chairs are required.

**Strengths:** living water, shade, existing platforms, strong river-household recognition, and an easy stationary boat threshold.

**Weaknesses:** roots, narrow approaches, limited kitchen access, poor dry turning space, and a risk that Tomas’s adoption visually overwhelms Neris’s entry into mortal household standing.

**Best use:** smaller ceremony with overflow witnesses on the market bridge or opposite bank. The Vale canopy, keys, or household act must remain clearly visible.

### Shrine rise and old ford

**Capacity:** thirty seated at the shrine, additional standing witnesses along the ford.

**Strengths:** neutral ground, dry shelter, existing runnel, clear officiant acoustics, and the fastest rain fallback.

**Weaknesses:** limited feast space, divided sight lines, little room for dance, and an uphill approach for several guests.

**Best use:** shortened compact-first order in hard rain, or separate consent and record at the shrine followed by a brief departure crossing at the ford.

No site is neutral. Name whose comfort, recognition, and labor each choice improves, and whose it spends. Then compensate with a shorter route, visible household act, carried announcement, second witnessing position, or private exchange.

## Wet and dry ground in one ceremony

The core construction is not a half-wet compromise surface. It is a sequence of adjacent surfaces whose use is explicit.

Dessa’s preferred module uses:

- dry plank paths for chairs, canes, shoes, and wheeled carts;
- low reed mats over firm ground for standing witnesses;
- shallow flowing rills no deeper than two fingers;
- basin chairs for guests who want moving water without unstable footing;
- broad crossings where the couple and attendants can turn without stepping backward; and
- screens at each return point to prevent wax, petals, pins, and food from entering the channel.

River guests differ in how much water they need. Deep-Reed needs feet in moving water but a dry backed chair. Lilt-before-Storm needs audible flow and can remain dry. Serein prefers to stand in a rill for the adoption act but does not require the entire ceremony there. Neris can cross dry ground for several minutes if the route and purpose are chosen rather than imposed. Mortal guests also differ. Aunt Sal wants the wet route with a handrail. Agnes wants stable dry ground and a clear view. Noll Ferry wants both dry footing and easy retreat from crowding.

The plan therefore marks **water positions**, **dry positions**, and **choice positions** rather than “river side” and “mortal side.” Guests can move only if they wish. Nobody is assigned to water by ancestry.

## The rill test

Assemble one rill section before choosing the whole plan.

1. Draw water from an allowed point above the site.
2. Run it through two trays and beneath one bridge section.
3. Place dry mats on both sides.
4. Test the flow with leaves, then remove every leaf at the return screen.
5. Have Agnes’s chair, Deep-Reed’s basin chair, a child, and a person carrying the compact chest pass or remain nearby.
6. Tip one tray, obstruct one return, and shift one mat to see what fails visibly.

Success demonstrates that one place can contain moving water and dry ground without pretending every person shares one surface. A partial failure identifies labor or capacity: a sagging mat, inaudible water, splashed hem, blocked chair turn, or return screen that needs a steward.

## The six-function plan

Dessa redraws the ceremony by function rather than prop. Place six visible stations or cues.

### Consent station

Both partners must be seen and heard without family members standing between them and the witnesses. The station needs no object. It needs quiet, clear sight, and a pause route if either answer changes.

At the meadow, place consent near the center before the household platforms. At the wheel yard, stop the wheel or move beyond its noise. At the willow bank, use the broad dry platform rather than forcing Tomas into the boat before he has publicly chosen the marriage.

### Household-standing station

This station may include keys, the threshold boat, a shared doorway frame, or spoken duties. It must allow retained standing to be visible as well as entry. If Tomas enters the boat, the route by which he leaves it should already be in place. If Neris accepts Vale household standing beneath the veil canopy, she must remain visible and uncovered.

### Name station

The announcer, Mera, and the couple need a clear speaking triangle. The record should not be read from behind the couple as though names are being assigned to them. A small water bowl and dry stone can hold witness marks, but neither is mandatory.

### Exchange station

Every accepted object needs a stable surface, correct giver, safe approach, and route away if refused or deferred. An empty place is useful. It makes a withheld gift visible without requiring explanation beyond the receiver’s stated choice.

### Promise station

The speakers need quiet and enough time for the chosen vow structure. The musicians should see Ansel’s cue but not play beneath words merely to maintain atmosphere. In rain, this station moves under roof first.

### Departure station

The departure path begins where the last promise ends and reaches a place the couple can occupy together. It cannot terminate at two separate family platforms. If the boat is used, it is placed perpendicular to the bank and secured at both ends so entry and exit occur before the same witnesses.

Dessa draws sight-line cones from each station to Agnes, Deep-Reed, the free witnesses, and overflow guests. Not everyone must see every hand movement. The six certifiable acts must each have enough direct witnesses that the record is credible.

## The threshold boat

The boat is seven feet long, broad-bottomed, and open at both ends. It draws less than a foot of water when Tomas stands inside. It is not fitted for travel and has no oars. The absence of oars is useful evidence: nobody planned a departure downriver.

The standard adoption sequence is:

1. The boat is tied perpendicular to the bank between two stable landings.
2. Tomas states that he enters under his own power to accept the bounded duties already recorded.
3. He steps in without being pulled or covered.
4. Neris or Serein receives him by naming the duties and the river household’s reciprocal obligations.
5. Tomas may refuse or correct any duty stated differently from the compact.
6. Neris joins him only if the couple chooses a paired threshold.
7. Both step out toward the shared departure route.

Alternatives include placing the open iron spiral on the boat’s side, using the boat only to hold the water bowl and adoption record, or omitting it entirely in favor of a bridge crossing. The boat is not valid merely because it is old custom. It is useful if it makes entry, receipt, reciprocity, and exit legible.

Safety requires handholds, shallow water, a dry bypass, and one named boat steward. Tomas should rehearse once in ordinary clothes. A surprise balance test is not a loyalty test.

## Procession patterns

The spatial plan must match the musical plan. Dessa offers three patterns.

### Paired approaches

The Vales and river household approach from different directions. Tomas and Neris may walk with their present households, alone, or already together. The approaches meet at the consent station. This makes both backgrounds visible but requires room and synchronized timing.

### One shared route with alternating offices

All guests enter by the same safe path. Different people lead portions: Mara at the mill gate, Rain at the first rill, Pella at the guest turn, Ansel at the shrine marker. This reduces distance and avoids a cultural parade, but household recognition must be carried through announced offices and acts.

### Gathered witnesses, moving couple

Guests are seated before the ceremony. Tomas and Neris move among six stations while families remain visible around them. This is accessible and weather-resistant. It can make the couple feel inspected unless they choose the movement and have a private pause route.

No procession is mandatory. In poor weather the couple can begin together at the central station and let names, objects, music, and speakers carry the distinctions.

## Labor and office assignment

Construction creates ceremonial offices that can satisfy real desires for recognition.

- Orren can lead bridge pegging and serve as threshold-boat steward.
- Mara can assign mill hands and certify that the work does not disrupt wheel safety.
- Aunt Sal can supervise handrails and guide guests over the wet route.
- Brin can label modules and must answer for any invented label that sends a guest wrong.
- Elsin can mark sight lines, test chest routes, and stop adults from calling her “the future miller” while she works.
- Rain can verify intake and return points and post water changes.
- Pella can confirm table and kitchen routes remain open.
- Noll Ferry can test crowd exits from the perspective of someone who needs quick air.

Do not spend the couple's eve hauling every module. Reassign labor before exhaustion begins making decisions for them.

## Yard complications

1. **The beautiful spiral.** A family sketch becomes popular until a chair cannot turn through it. Preserve the spiral as lantern pattern or discard it.
2. **The dry rill.** The first test is too quiet for Lilt-before-Storm. Increasing flow splashes Agnes’s route. A separate audible spillway solves the need better than widening every channel.
3. **The ceremonial depth.** Serein remembers the adoption boat in deeper water. Tomas can accept the same duty in shallower depth; the witnesses must distinguish symbolic intensity from actual requirement.
4. **The uncredited crew.** Guests praise the river for the platforms while workers are still carrying them. Dessa stops work until names, wages, and feast seats are entered.
5. **The blocked mill lane.** A grand approach prevents flour carts from moving. Shorten it, move the wheel schedule, or choose another site.
6. **The moved peg.** Children relocate a lantern stake and expose that everyone has been using decoration as a navigation marker. Replace it with a labeled structural cue.
7. **The high water rehearsal.** A sudden release raises the test trough. The modules hold, but one return screen clogs, proving the need for a named water steward.

## Decisions that travel forward

Record:

- primary and fallback sites;
- capacity at each site and who may witness from overflow positions;
- the position of each of the six functions;
- wet, dry, and choice positions for named guests;
- rill intake, return, screen, and water steward;
- handrails, chairs, turning spaces, and retreat routes;
- whether and how the threshold boat is used;
- the procession pattern and joining point;
- module labels, labor assignments, movement time, and the deadline for relocation; and
- which decorations are sacrificed first if weather or labor worsens.

Take the plan to the Bridge of Three Tunes for timing and cues. Test it at the Flood Meadow with actual guest stand-ins, objects, and a simulated site change.

## Connections

- Return to the **House of Open Measure** if the physical plan exposes an unstated household consequence.
- Confirm keys, work lanes, and Vale household acts at **Vale Mill and Hearth**.
- Confirm adoption wording, water positions, and reciprocal duties at the **House Beneath the Willows**.
- Bring guest capacity, chairs, lodging routes, and gift handling from the **Market of Seven Baskets**.
- Use the **Shrine of the Open Door** six-function order as the plan’s skeleton.
- Coordinate processions and movable joining points at the **Bridge of Three Tunes**.
- Conduct the full load, weather, and sight-line test at the **Flood Meadow and Old Ford**.

## If the yard is skipped or reached late

Use a known safe fixed site. The shrine rise and old wheel yard can each support a stripped ceremony without a moving rill, threshold boat, elaborate ramps, or late structural improvisation. Mark wet and dry standing places with existing ground, mats, benches, and spoken office rather than unstable devices.

Dessa's absence removes craft capacity, not ceremonial meaning. Consent, names, promises, and departure remain possible. Household standing and exchange must be made legible through words and accepted acts instead of architecture. The couple takes its first shared step on a route they have inspected.

A late safety discovery can stop an object, route, or structure immediately. It cannot dictate the marriage. Move the affected function, omit the device, reduce attendance, or relocate. Do not ask a last-minute roll to determine whether a visibly unsafe platform somehow holds.

## Failure forward

Bad planning produces wet clothes, separated audiences, a delayed start, omitted decoration, tired workers, or an improvised ceremony at the old ford. A site change may reduce the guest count or move one exchange private. None of these outcomes invalidates freely chosen promises.

The physical plan becomes unacceptable only when it prevents a principal from choosing, hearing, moving safely, or understanding what the ceremony publicly claims. Even then, Dessa can strip the design to dry shelter, one moving-water basin, six visible functions, and a shared departure. A smaller honest place is better than an impressive structure whose bodies contradict its words.
